Some teachers say, 'If one wears a robe without applying a smudge mark (kappabindu), he does not become one in communion by theft (theyyasaṃvāsaka)'; this should be investigated. 'Liṅgānurūpassa' means because of enjoying the communion that is suitable for a novice (sāmaṇera).
25: For those who have assumed the guise of a monk due to fear of the king or other dangers, even if they possess a deceptive intent such as "Let people recognize me as a monk," it should be understood that no fault is incurred because they lack the intent to deceive the monks or the desire to associate in communion with them. If one acts without knowing that "one who goes forth in this manner is called a theyya-saṃvāsaka (one who lives in communion by theft)," or "it is not permissible to do so," or "one who goes forth in this way is not a novice (sāmaṇera)," then it is permissible. However, it is recorded that if one acts while knowing, it is not permissible. It is held that: "One who dons the robes for the purpose of escaping danger from the king, famine, etc., and finds gratification in communion, becomes a theyya-saṃvāsaka due to having an impure mind. Furthermore, if that person later develops a pure mind, thinking, 'I will practice the pure holy life; what is the use of living in communion by theft?' either out of remorse or because of the ease of obtaining the four requisites, and as long as he does not accept (engage in or find gratification in) that communion, he is not yet a theyya-saṃvāsaka. From the moment such a pure thought arises, if he then finds gratification in communion, he becomes a theyya-saṃvāsaka." Some teachers state that otherwise, everything would be contradictory. It is said: "If a biological son, born from the stroking of the mother's navel etc., kills his biological father, he becomes a pitu-ghātaka (paticide)." A person who causes the destruction of virtue through physical contact is not a bhikkhunī-dūsaka (corrupter of a nun) because of the statement regarding the "three paths." However, there is a decision that even if one corrupts a nun who has been ordained by only one side (ekato-upasampanna), he becomes a bhikkhunī-dūsaka and is also subject to pārājika (defeat). Although it is not explicitly mentioned in the commentaries, Vinaya experts accept that a nun can also be a theyya-saṃvāsikā, a mother-killer, a father-killer, an arahant-killer, one who sheds the blood of a Buddha, or one who has gone over to a non-Buddhist sect. A monk who does not transgress the limit taught as "There is an offense of pācittiya for deliberate lying" is said to be one who trains in that training rule (sikkhāpada). A training rule is merely a designation (paññatti) and not an ultimate reality (paramattha); here, the regulation is intended. It is written with reference to the meaning stated in the Samantapāsādikā: "This training rule is a designation for restraint from sexual intercourse." Sikkhā (training) refers to the arising of the mental state (cittuppāda) that proceeds with the nature of training in various training rules. Sājīva (the code of discipline) is the regulation (paññatti). To demonstrate that meaning, it was previously said: "This is a designation for restraint from sexual intercourse." Since there is no lineage (tanti) of training that is regarded as virtue or merit, the "declaration of weakness" (dubbalya-vikamma) to laypeople is not possible in that training. Indeed, that training is something to be desired; therefore, it is stated in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary: "Having reached that sājīva, without declaring the state of weakness in that sājīva." Elder Upatissa stated that weakness is possible in the training rule (sikkhāpada) which is an authoritative regulation. The term dubbalya-vikamma should be understood either as a euphonic word or as a supplementary term for the preceding phrase indicating the abandonment of the training, similar to phrases like diratta tiratta. Otherwise, since in some cases of discarding the training, the declaration of weakness is not required, the Buddha said "without declaring weakness" with the intention of explaining the meaning of the term "without renouncing the training" (sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāya). Stopping at that phrase...
26:
## 
"One who is possessed of the shared livelihood (sājīva) without revealing his state of weakness in that shared livelihood," is stated in the Kankhā Commentary (Kankhā-aṭṭhakathā). The Elder Upatissa stated that weakness can occur in a training rule that is a command (āṇā). The term 'revealing weakness' (dubbalyāvikamma) should be understood either as a smooth linguistic expression for the phrase showing the renunciation of the training, or as a supplementary phrase.

Alternatively, because in the act of disrobing, some do not clearly reveal their state of weakness, and intending to refer to that lack of revelation, the author said "without revealing weakness" (dubbalyaṃ anāvikattvā) to explain the meaning of the phrase "without renouncing the training" (sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāya). In that statement, if one asks: "Since not every revelation of weakness is a renunciation of training, should one not first say 'without revealing weakness' and then say 'without renouncing the training' to define the meaning of that phrase?" That is not appropriate. Why? Because there would be no sequence of meaning. Since the Buddha said, "one possessed of the training and shared livelihood" (sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno), the commentary's statement, "one who is possessed of such training, without renouncing that training; and one who is possessed of such shared livelihood, without revealing weakness in that shared livelihood," expresses the meaning according to the sequence of the Buddha's words. It should not be stated in any other sequence. Therefore, this phrase "without renouncing the training" is stated first. "Of those very ones" (tesaṃyeva) refers to the fourteen types of persons. In order to make this phrase "without renouncing the training" applicable to all training rules, it is stated in the commentary: "This is the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) in this training rule."

'Insertion' (pavesana) means the contact of the male organ with the path of entry by one who is inserting it. 'Entered' (paviṭṭha) refers to the incomplete period or the period of effort by one who is inserting it as far as the base. At the time of the emission of semen, the male organ is called 'stationary' (ṭhita). 'Withdrawal' (uddharaṇa) refers to the time of taking out the male organ. In the Vinaya-gaṇṭhipada, however, it is said: "Ceasing from effort and remaining still is called 'stationary'." I have stated this to show it without confusion. Even during the times of insertion, being entered, and withdrawal, the emission of semen certainly occurs. 'Gratification' (sādiyana) means the arising of the thought of indulgence or the thought of acceptance and enjoyment.

Referring to the training rules prescribed only in the Ubhatovibhaṅga, it is said: "This is the introduction (nidāna) to all training rules." Because it is said, "Ordination (upasampadā) by a group with a Vinaya-holder as the fifth," the third case ending (instrumental) is used here in the sense of association (saha). Therefore, even if twenty monks are sitting, only the fifth one is desired to be a Vinaya-holder. In such a case, if that Vinaya-holder has committed a Pārajika offense, does it invalidate the act of ordination (upasampadā-kamma)? No, it does not. Why? Because in the Kammavagga at the end of the Parivāra, the characteristics of the failure of a kamma are stated, and those characteristics of failure are not present in that [Pārajika monk]. It is stated: "How [is it a failure]? By way of the object (vatthu), the motion (ñatti), the proclamation (anussāvana), the boundary (sīmā), or the assembly (parisā)." If one asks: "Is this [Pārajika monk] not included in the words 'by way of the assembly'?" No, he is not. Why? Because in the detailed analysis (Vibhaṅga) of the verse stating "By twelve ways, kammas fail due to the assembly," that monk who has committed a Pārajika is not included.
27:
## 
Because that [Pārajika monk] is not touched upon (not mentioned) in the Vibhaṅga of the Sutta, this meaning can only be known by the power of the Pali text as specifically stated in various places. Therefore, a brief indication of the method is written. Extracting the word "factor" (aṅga), it is said: "In all training rules, the factors and non-factors of the offenses should be known." Why is only "factor" (aṅga) mentioned here [in the Kankhāvitaraṇī]? Because originations (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth appear briefly in the Parivāra and other texts, they are taken from there; and because there is no limit to the non-factors (anaṅga) pointed out here; and because if non-factors were stated in brief and in detail for all training rules, it would be too extensive, as they must be stated fully for each specific training rule. It should be understood that [only factors are mentioned] by way of being inclusive of all offenses.

By the power of the training rules called "action" (kiriya), the body and speech together with intimation (viññatti) should be understood. By the power of "non-action" (akiriya), they should be understood without intimation. Here, the mind (citta) is not the measure, because the origination of Bhūtārocana (announcing superhuman states) is both an action (kiriya) and is also [sometimes] mindless (acittaka). In that [Bhūtārocana], the action should be understood as having an intermediate mind that is not a factor of the offense as its cause. Even though it does not produce intimation, some training rules are called "action" (kiriya) by way of common usage (bāhulla-naya), just like the first Pārajika. Even in the absence of intimation, it is said: "If he gratifies, it is a Pārajika offense; if he does not gratify, there is no offense." The action called intimation (viññatti) also cannot occur without the mind of indulgence, because it is produced by the mind, is a form of alteration (vikāra-rūpa), and follows the mind. Therefore, this intimation-form called action, like other mind-produced matter, cannot exist without the producing mind. Other sense-bases of sound (saddāyatana), however, do exist. Therefore, when there is action, there is definitely the mind of indulgence that produces it; thus, the statement "if he does not gratify, there is no offense" would be inappropriate [if action alone were the criteria]. Since the mind of indulgence, even while being the producer of intimation, does not produce intimation at all times, it can arise by itself even without intimation; therefore, the Buddha taught: "If he gratifies, it is a Pārajika offense." If [the mind of indulgence] does not arise, it is called 'not gratifying', and for him, there is no offense. For this very reason, the Blessed One determines the offense by the mind alone, saying, "Monk, what was your intention (citta)?" It should be understood that He does not determine it by the action (kiriya) alone.

In this context, the inclusion of 'origination' (samuṭṭhāna) serves the purpose of showing that an offense is committed only with regard to the distinction of body and so forth, whether as something to be done or something not to be done, and not otherwise. Among those [originations, etc.], the inclusion of 'action' (kiriya) serves the purpose of showing the distinction between having intimation and not having intimation of the body and so forth. The inclusion of 'perception' (saññā) serves the purpose of showing the distinction between the mind that is a factor of the offense and the mind that is not a factor.
28:
Therefore, the mind that is established in the characteristic of action (kiriya) or non-action (akiriya), or the mind from which action or non-action arises, is not, in a general sense, a factor or a non-factor of an offense. Rather, it is shown that the mind associated with the perception called "release through perception" (saññāvimokkha) is a factor, while the mind not associated with it is not a factor.

Now, a training rule is "with mind" (sacittaka) because of a certain mind; in the absence of that mind, it is "without mind" (acittaka). Because of the general faultiness of that training rule through that mind, it is said to be "only a worldly fault" (lokavajja). However, although they are equally faulty, the term "cittalokavajja" is used for the purpose of showing that some training rules are worldly faults (lokavajja) and some are faults by regulation (paṇṇattivajja). Since only the mind is called "worldly fault," the term "action" (kamma) is included to prevent the undesirable implication that mental action (manokamma) could also be an offense.

In this context, the kusalatika (triad of the wholesome) is included to prevent the undesirable implication that an action with the characteristic of non-action might be excluded from the kusalatika. The vedanātika (triad of feeling) is included to prevent the thought that it is not applicable here, since some indeterminate (abyākata) offenses can be committed even by one who has entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), despite being devoid of feeling. Although a training rule is called "having three minds and three feelings" based on a person "with mind" (sacittaka), an offense committed "without mind" (acittaka) is also called "having three minds and three feelings." Regarding this, there is the supporting Sutta passage: "There is an offense that one without mind (acittaka) commits and from which one without mind emerges" (Parivāra 324), and "There is an offense that one with a wholesome mind commits and from which one with a wholesome mind emerges" (Parivāra 470). The teacher Vajirabuddhi wrote: "Sacittaka indicates an offense; saññāvimokkha indicates the absence of an offense; acittaka means not knowing the object; nosaññāvimokkha means knowing the transgression. This is the difference between those perceptions and minds."

In the phrase "in the side of with-mind" (sacittakapakkhé), here is the method of the Gaṇṭhipada: sacittakapakkhé is said with reference to "without-mind" (acittaka) training rules such as drinking intoxicants (surāpāna). Among "with-mind" training rules, those that arise solely from an unwholesome mind and those that are both sacittaka and acittaka are called worldly faults (lokavajja). In the training rule of drinking intoxicants, drinking while knowing "it is liquor" or "it is not proper to drink" is purely unwholesome. In that context, the statement "knowing it is not proper" is inappropriate because it would imply that a fault by regulation (paṇṇattivajja) also becomes a worldly fault (lokavajja). To avoid this undesirable implication, the Elder Vajirabuddhi wrote: "In this matter, the investigation of 'with-mind' and 'without-mind' occurs only in knowing the object (vatthu), not in knowing the regulation (paññatti)."
29:
If knowing the regulation were the criterion, then all training rules would be worldly faults (lokavajja). But not all training rules are worldly faults. Therefore, the statement that (the investigation) occurs only in knowing the object (vatthu) is appropriate. Why? Because in the Sekhiya training rules, only the knowing of the regulation is the standard, not the mere knowing of the object.

The meaning here is: taking the offense by way of the training rule, if the mind of a "with-mind" (sacittaka) training rule is only unwholesome, that training rule is called a worldly fault (lokavajja). Also, in an "without-mind" (acittaka) training rule (which is categorized as both sacittaka and acittaka), if the mind is only unwholesome in the "with-mind" portion, that "without-mind" training rule is also a worldly fault, like drinking intoxicants (surāpāna). With reference to this meaning, it is said: "If the mind is only unwholesome in the with-mind portion of a training rule, this training rule is called a worldly fault." Indeed, the phrase "in the side of with-mind" (sacittakapakkhé) is said with reference to "without-mind" (acittaka) training rules. For there is no purpose in using the qualifier "in the side of with-mind" for a rule that is purely "with-mind." This being so, the meaning is that a statement made indefinitely should be understood definitely.

In the phrase "But of animals" (tiracchānānaṃ pana), the word "but" (pana) excludes offenses such as thullaccaya. In the word "action" (kiriya), if it is asked how that is so, since it is said "he consents to what is stationary" (Pārājika 58)? Because it is said "he consents," it is indeed an action (kiriya). If so, should it not be called "bodily action and mental action"? No, because it is called "bodily action" according to common usage. It is written that in the ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā training rule of the Bhikkhunī Pārājika, action (kiriya) is indeed obtained. It should be understood by comparing it with the method mentioned previously. The Blessed One, who said, "Monks, when the words and syllables are poorly laid down, the meaning is also difficult to understand" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.20), desired the proper placement of words and syllables only for the sake of easily grasping the meaning. He did not desire the mere recitation of letters. Therefore, it is said, "The Lord declared the meaning alone as the refuge," and so on.

## The Explanation of the First Pārājika is Finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Second Pārājika

"Whether from a village or from a forest" is stated at the beginning because it is a supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) that characterizes the Pārājika case. In the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, the classification of "village" (gāma) should be understood as fivefold: the village, the precinct of the village, the territory of the village (gāmakhetta), the village boundary (gāmasīmā), and the precinct of the village boundary. Similarly, in the division of "forest" (arañña), there is one forest that is not a village, one forest mentioned in the saṃvidhāna training rules (Pācittiya 180, etc.), and one forest that is with a village...
30:
The classification of forest should be understood as being of five kinds: one (associated with a village), one in an avippavāsa-sīmā, and one for a bhikkhunī left behind by a group (Pācittiya 691). Among those villages and forests, it should also be understood that in some training rules, there is a village that does not receive the protection of a village, and there is a village that does not perform the functions of a village. Similarly, there is a forest that does not receive the protection of a forest, and there is a forest that does not perform the functions of a forest.

Among those villages and forests, in the formal act (kammavācā) for designating an avippavāsa-sīmā, in the phrase "excluding the village and the precinct (upacāra) of the village" (Mahāvagga 144), a village should be understood as the interior of the enclosure if it is enclosed, and the interior of the site of the enclosure if it is not enclosed. This village appears as "inside the village" (antogāma) in the Udositā training rule (Pārājika 478). In the Sāsaṅka training rule, it appears without doubt as "inside the houses" (antaraghara) (Pārājika 654). This is as the Buddha said: "To place inside the houses means to place in the surrounding gocara-gāma" (Pārājika 654). Similarly, this same delimitation should be understood in the Sekhiya training rules related to "inside the houses". In the training rule "Whatever bhikkhunī should go alone to another village" (Pācittiya 687), this same delimitation is intended because it is stated: "for one crossing the enclosure of an enclosed village, for one crossing the precinct (upacāra) of an unenclosed village".

In those ancient manuscripts where it is written "for one entering (okkama) the precinct", it is not authoritative (correct) because it was written through negligence, taking the method practiced in the training rules for entering a village at the wrong time (vikāla). In those manuscripts where, in the analysis (vibhaṅga) of the training rule for entering a village at the wrong time (Pācittiya 513), it is written "To enter a village means for one crossing the enclosure of an enclosed village, for one crossing the precinct of an unenclosed village", that is merely a scribal error. The correct reading there is "for one entering (okkama) the precinct". Indeed, it is stated in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary: "The precinct of an unenclosed village should be understood in the same manner as stated in the training rule on taking what is not given" (Pācittiya Commentary 512). In this Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary also, it is stated: "Without asking a monk who is present... for one entering the precinct", etc.

In some manuscripts, regarding the bhikkhunīs' going to another village, the reading is found: "If one crosses the enclosure or enters the precinct of another village with one foot, a thullaccaya [offence]; as soon as one has crossed or entered with the second foot, a saṅghādisesa." In that reading, these words "enters, as soon as one has entered"...
31:
...found in the reading "bhikkhuniyā... saṅghādiseso", these words "okkante okkantamatte" (enters, as soon as one has entered) are redundant. These words do not belong to the Elders of the Councils but were written only by other scribes. In some manuscripts, the word "okkantamatte ca" is not found, but another word is found. Both types of words contradict the Pali text. This is because in the Pali text, there is only "apari-kkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ atikkamantiyā" (for one crossing the precinct of an unenclosed village). Similarly, they also contradict the Samantapāsādikā Commentary. In that commentary, it is stated: "If one crosses with one foot the place suitable for an enclosure, a thullaccaya offence; if one crosses with the second foot, a saṅghādisesa offence is incurred. Furthermore, here, from one's own village... if one crosses with one foot either the enclosure or the precinct of another village, a thullaccaya offence; as soon as one crosses with the second foot, a saṅghādisesa offence is incurred."

In the Gaṇṭhipada of that training rule also, it is stated "parikkhepaṃ atikkamantiyā" (for one crossing the enclosure) and "in the precinct also, the method is the same". In the Anugaṇṭhipada also, it is stated: "In some manuscripts, 'okkamantiyā' (entering) is found for the precinct of an unenclosed village; that view should not be accepted." Another point is also stated: "By the words 'apari-kkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ atikkamantiyā', it should be understood thus: In entering a village at the wrong time (vikāla), the precinct should be delimited only by the distance of two clod-throws. Otherwise, if the meaning were taken [differently], just as in this training rule it is said 'atikkamantiyā' (crossing) by treating the place suitable for an enclosure as an enclosure, so too in that training rule for entering a village at the wrong time, it would say 'apari-kkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ atikkamantassa'. However, in that training rule, the precinct is intended as the distance of one clod-throw beyond the place suitable for an enclosure. Therefore, to show that meaning, it was stated 'apari-kkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ okkamantassa' (for one entering the precinct of an unenclosed village)."

In the Andhaka Commentary, having noted only the place suitable for an enclosure as the precinct, it was stated "for one entering the precinct" to show the lack of difference between the enclosure and the place suitable for an enclosure. Without noting the specific distinction in the Pali, the statement "For one crossing the precinct of an unenclosed village, here the precinct should be like an enclosure; if one crosses that precinct with the first foot, a dukkaṭa offence; if one crosses with the second foot, a pācittiya offence is incurred" should not be accepted because of the existence of the specific distinction in the Pali. In the ancient Gaṇṭhipada, it is stated: "For a bhikkhunī crossing the precinct, a gāmantara offence is incurred." Therefore, in this Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary, only this reading "with one foot... as soon as one has crossed, a saṅghādisesa offence is incurred" should be understood. By this much, in these aforementioned instances, only the aforementioned delimitation should be understood as the village (gāma).
32:
## 
To clarify this meaning, it has been stated: "A village may even consist of a single house" and so forth (Pārājika Pali, 92). By virtue of this meaning, even if there is no crossing of a fence or entering the precinct, for a monk entering that village from within a monastery, or from a nunnery, or from a titthiya's dwelling, or from a refectory, offenses based on the village are to be understood as occurring due to crossing the enclosure or precinct of the monastery's interior.

The village precinct (gāmūpacāra), in the context of "excluding the village and the village precinct" (regarding the designation of a boundary for not being separated from the three robes), is the fence itself if the village is fenced; if the village is unfenced, it is the space where a fence would be. Thus, it is stated in the Mahāvagga Commentary: "The village precinct is the fence of a fenced village, and the space for a fence of an unfenced village. In those places, a monk who has determined his three robes does not receive the privilege (parihāra) [of being separated from them]." Why is the village and its precinct defined one way here and another way elsewhere? Because of the origin of the story (aṭṭhuppatti): "At that time, monks, thinking 'The Blessed One has allowed the formal agreement for not being separated from the three robes,' were leaving their robes inside the village." Due to this origin, it was stated: "excluding the village and the village precinct." Therefore, it should be understood that where the perception of 'inside the village' exists, the boundary for not being separated from the robes does not extend.

Hence, in the Udosita training rule, it is stated: "Having left the robe inside the village, one should stay within the village itself," and "In a rest house or at the foot of a gate, one should not be separated [from the robe] beyond the reach of a hand." This is because only one staying in a suitable place can guard a robe placed in a suitable place. However, in the Sāsaṅka training rule, it is said: "Since a person staying away from the village where the robe is kept is said to be separated from the robe, one should enter the village boundary, stay there, and then depart." In that training rule, the village boundary (gāmasīmā) is intended as the "village" (gāma).

Among these, in the analysis (vibhaṅga) of the training rule on entering a village at an improper time: "For a monk crossing the fence of a fenced village, there is an offense of pācittiya." By this statement, it is hinted that the fence is not the village, but rather the village precinct (gāmūpacāra). In the analysis of this (second Pārājika) training rule, starting with "What is called the village precinct," it is established by the words "the distance of a stone's throw by a man of average strength standing at the precinct of a house in an unfenced village" that the space where a fence would be in an unfenced village is the village precinct. Because that meaning is possible, the distance of a stone's throw by one standing in the precinct of that house is the village precinct, as stated in the Kurundī Commentary and the Mahāpaccari...
33:
...it is stated in the Commentary. For "precinct" (upacāra) in such phrases as "a village with one precinct or many precincts" means a gate; in the passage "an open space with one precinct," it refers to the measurement known as seven abbhantaras in all directions. Therefore, it should be understood as stated in the Andhaka Commentary: "The village precinct is the fence of a fenced village, and the space for a fence of an unfenced village." The same is stated in the Kurundī and the Mahāpaccari. Likewise, in the Pali texts, it is seen in passages such as: "Ajjhārāma means the interior of a fenced monastery, and the precinct of an unfenced monastery; ajjhāvasatha means the interior of a fenced dwelling, and the precinct of an unfenced dwelling." However, in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is seen in "gāmūpacāra" and so forth. Therefore, the second stone's throw is intended as the precinct.

Because of the specific Pali text: "For a monk entering the precinct of an unfenced village, there is an offense of pācittiya," it is said that the first stone's throw is the village itself, and the second stone's throw is the village precinct. For a fenced village, it is stated that the distance of a stone's throw by a man of average strength standing at the threshold (indakhīla) is the village precinct; there is no difference here. By this much, the two types of precincts for a fenced village and the four types of precincts for an unfenced village are shown, where they occur and where they do not. The characteristics of the village field (gāmakhetta) and the village boundary (gāmasīmā) are stated in the Commentary itself. Both are one in meaning. In that context, the status of the village boundary as a village is to be understood by virtue of the Sāsaṅka training rule.

The precinct of the village boundary (gāmasīmūpacāra) is the place used by people seeking wood, grass, flowers, fruits, etc., and by forest-dwellers. The status of this place as a village boundary precinct is to be understood from the Udosita training rule and from the Mahāvagga Khandhaka (147) where it says: "in a forest where there is no village, seven abbhantaras all around." For here, the Blessed One, wishing to show the boundary for monks living in a village, showed it by saying: "depending on whatever village or market town he dwells." Immediately after that, He showed the seven-abbhantara boundary with "in a place where there is no village" and so forth. Therefore, if a monk does not dwell depending on a village or market town, but is merely traveling a long distance by boat or by land, it should be understood that he obtains the seven-abbhantara boundary in those various places. It is said: "A caravan of a single family..."
34:
## 
“There is a caravan of a single family; all monks, having laid aside their robes, should not be separated from them within seven usabhas, whether in front or behind,” and so forth, as stated in the Pārājika (489). Referring specifically to this type of forest, it was said: “a forest that is not a village within a forest boundary (araññaka-sīmā).”

Referring to which forest it was stated in the Pācittiya Pali (414): “In a forest that is not a village, an offense of pācittiya is incurred for every half-league (yojana).” This is known as the forest that is not a village in the context of the Saṃvidhāna training rules.

Specifically, by the previous statement (from the Udositā training rule), a forest with houses (sagāma) is included; by this statement (from the Saṃvidhāna training rule), that forest with houses is not included. Referring to that forest (with houses), in the commentary regarding the matter of leaving the group (gaṇamhā ohīyana) (Pācittiya Commentary 692), it is stated: “In the phrase ‘agāmake araññe,’ the forest is defined by the characteristic that ‘everything outside after exiting the village threshold (indakhīla) is called forest.’ However, it is called ‘agāmaka’ (non-village) simply because of the absence of a village, not because it resembles the Vinjha forest.” Referring to which forest it was taught: “A forest dwelling (āraṇyaka-senāsana) must be at least five hundred bow-lengths (dhanu) away” (Pārājika 654, Pācittiya 573). This so-called forest dwelling is the forest, whether with trees or without trees, located outside the enclosure of a fenced village, or outside the space designated for an enclosure in an unfenced village; even if it is interspersed with small rivers and streams within a monastery, it is called arañña (forest). Likewise, it was taught: “one forest for one who leaves the group.” This too is indeed a forest. Specifically, this forest (mentioned in the Gaṇa-ohīyana) possesses the characteristics already mentioned in the context of being a non-village; after exiting the village threshold, at the moment of leaving the sight-reach (dassanūpacāra), it causes a (saṅghādisesa) offense only once, and thereafter no offense is incurred. However, the forest described as “one forest of the Saṃvidhāna training rules” causes an offense for every half-league, but not within that half-league. The other three types of forests do not fulfill the procedure stated for that forest within the aforementioned limits, but fulfill it only outside those limits. Thus, the mutual differences between these five types of forests should be understood.

Among those five types of villages and forests, the village precinct (gāmūpacāra) described as “a stone’s throw (leḍḍupāta) of one standing at the threshold (indakhīla) of a fenced village” (Pārājika 92) is not utilized anywhere in the Vinaya Piṭaka; it was taught only for the purpose of showing that another stone’s throw distance from the space designated for an enclosure in an unfenced village is called the village precinct. If it is said that one stone’s throw from a fenced village is also a precinct similar to a suitable ground (kappiya-bhūmi), then one stone’s throw from the designated enclosure space of an unfenced village is certainly a precinct from the start. That precinct (of two stone’s throws), because it is distinct and is an open space, causes an offense to one who enters it.
35:
## 
Excluding the gāmantara offense of a bhikkhunī, an offense is caused to one who enters (that second stone’s throw precinct). The reason is that while bhikkhunīs reside in that village precinct known as the second stone’s throw, they incur an offense, and when entering the village, they also incur a gāmantara offense. For according to the words: “At that very moment the shadow should be measured... the three dependencies and eight things not to be done (akaraṇīya) should be told to that bhikkhunī” (Cullavagga 430), the place where those bhikkhunīs stand is reckoned as forest. Because the training rules connected with the forest and the training rule on entering a village at the wrong time (vikāla-gāmapavesana) are not common (asādhāraṇa) to bhikkhunīs, and because it is said that the bhikkhunī quarters and refectories within a monastery are suitable grounds (kappiya-bhūmi), and because of the training rule: “If she should leave the group alone... in a forest without a village, for a bhikkhunī who leaves the sight-reach or hearing-reach of the second companion bhikkhunī, there is an offense of thullaccaya” (Pācittiya 692), or by the method of the Bhikkhunī-khandhaka, for whatever reason, the robe-carrying (ticīvarika) is permitted starting from the threshold of a fenced village or from the precinct of an unfenced village. At that time, if there is a robe deposited inside the village, monks reside (without offense) through the combination of the four factors; therefore, it is called sagāmaka (associated with a village).

As a single point regarding the avippavāsa-sīmā, according to the words: “Monks, a bhikkhunī should not live in the forest; for one who should live there, there is an offense of dukkaṭa” (Cullavagga 431), it is established that there is no such thing as living in the forest for bhikkhunīs. This is because even if that bhikkhunī is in a bhikkhunī quarters in the forest, she incurs an offense if she leaves the sight or hearing reach of the second companion even within the monastery. Therefore, in the phrase “excluding the village and the village precinct” in the context of the avippavāsa-sīmā (Mahāvagga 144), whatever village and village precinct are excluded, only in that village and village precinct is a bhikkhunī quarters also permissible, and not beyond that.

And because the words “excluding the village and the village precinct” are not present in the kammavācā for the avippavāsa-sīmā of those bhikkhunīs, the boundary extends only to those villages and village precincts. Beyond that, in the second stone’s throw etc., because it is unsuitable ground for them, the samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā (boundary of common communion) does not extend into the forest for them, just as the boundary for monks does not extend into the village and village precinct. Therefore, it was said: “excluding the gāmantara offense of a bhikkhunī.”

Having thus understood the five types of villages and the types of forests, now the distinctions such as “there is a village, but in some places it does not receive the status of a village” should be understood. Among those distinctions, that village which is described in the commentary as “amanussa means a place where humans are entirely absent and is possessed by yakkhas,” does not receive the status of a village in some training rules. For, referring to that village, the commentary states: “That village, in the time of the Buddha...”
36:
It has been stated (in the Pārājika Commentary, etc.) that "In the time of a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch), it is a city; at other times, it is desolate and possessed by yakkhas (spirits)." A village that has disappeared along with its houses, whether due to being plundered by rival kings or thieves, or simply abandoned out of fear, gives rise to the Pācittiya offense stated as "a Pācittiya offense in every interval between villages." It should be understood that it also gives rise to the offense for entering a village at the wrong time (after noon), and the four offenses in the Sekhiya rules. A village where people have departed with the intention of returning for some business is considered the same as a normal village.

In the statement "There is a forest, but nowhere does it receive the benefits of a forest," it should be understood that this refers to a forest with a separate precinct (upacāra), as stated: "In a forest without a village, a single precinct is seven abbhantaras all around; beyond that is a separate precinct." A village precinct (gāmūpacāra) consisting of a stone's throw from a fenced village, or a merchant caravan (sattha) established for no more than four months, though they are villages, they do not perform the functions of a village. One who enters such a place does not incur the offense of entering a village. A forest that is part of the village boundary and used by people, though it is a forest, does not perform the functions of a forest, because a forest boundary (āraññakasīmā) cannot be obtained there. By this much, the nature of the "characteristic sub-rule" (lakkhaṇānupaññatti) of the sub-rule "from a village or from a forest" is shown.

In the statement "A village established in a cattle pen, etc.," if that village has a defined village field (gāmakhetta), the whole is a single village. If not, it should be defined by its precinct or its fence. Even if there is a village field, if some houses are built far apart so that their precincts do not reach each other, the precinct alone is the standard for entering a village at the wrong time. For the Sekhiya rules related to the interior of a house and for a bhikkhunī's offenses of traveling between villages, the area suitable for fencing the houses is the standard. For acts such as the Uposatha, the village field is the standard. For a forest dwelling, the standard is a distance of five hundred bows starting from the second stone's throw of the nearest house—thus the teachers say we have this understanding.

"Even in a single village field, if the king demarcates a portion saying 'Let this also be a visuṃgāma (separate village)' and gives it to someone, that place is also a visuṃgāma boundary..."
37:
According to the words of the Mahāvagga Commentary (page 147), "It is indeed so," a bhikkhunī who enters such a visuṃgāma boundary alone indeed incurs the offense of traveling between villages (gāmantara-gamana). Even if there is no monastery, shrine, rest house, or house in that visuṃgāma, and it is merely a plot of land without buildings, it is still suitable to perform all Vinaya acts there as a visuṃgāma. For has the Blessed One not said, "A village without humans"? If that visuṃgāma area is within the fence or precinct of another village, one must ask permission before entering at the wrong time. If it is not (within the fence or precinct of another village), one may go as one pleases, as if going to a forest. If there is a park (ārāma) or one of the dwellings of non-Buddhists (titthiya) in that visuṃgāma, it is indeed permissible. If there is a bhikkhunī's residence, a bhikkhunī entering the village for alms should avoid the offense of traveling between villages.

In this passage (Pārājika, page 92), "A forest is that which remains after excluding the village and the village precinct," the meaning is: if there is a fence, excluding only the village with the stated boundaries, its precinct and beyond is called a forest; if there is no fence, excluding only the village precinct with the stated boundaries, the remaining area beyond that is called a forest. Only if it is so will the Vinaya procedures be consistent, such as: incurring an offense for separating from the group in a non-village forest with the characteristic "all this is a forest after stepping outside the threshold (indakhīla)"; the spreading of the boundary of non-separation (avippavāsasīmā) there; and the non-offense for entering a village at the wrong time. Otherwise, they would not be consistent.

When it is said, "A forest is that which remains after excluding the village precinct," since it is established that beyond the village precinct is the forest, is it not useless to specifically say "excluding the village"? If you ask, "Is it said for fear that the village might become a forest?" No, it is for fear that the village precinct might cease to exist. This is because a village precinct can only exist if there is a village. According to your view, that village precinct is a forest. If so, where would the village precinct be? If the village precinct is also counted as a forest, it is not proper to assume the village is separate (from the forest), nor is it proper to fear the village becoming a forest. Therefore, in the passage "from a village or from a forest," the village precinct is also included as "village." Thus, the fear of the village becoming a forest is not appropriate. If so, should it not be said only as "A forest is that which remains after excluding the village"? No, because it would then be difficult to know the boundary of the forest. The statement "The boundary of the forest is not clear" is our view. Here, the area ending at the village precinct is called the village. If so, while the Commentary should say, "It is said for the purpose of showing the boundary of the village and the boundary of the forest," why does it say, "It is said for the purpose of showing the boundary of the forest"?
38: If it is asked, "For what purpose is this said?" the answer is: the commentator said, "for the purpose of showing the boundary of the forest," referring only to the first village precinct. Indeed, in all training rules, starting from the outer threshold (indakhīla), the village precinct is called "forest" (arañña). Here, there is no purpose in stating the boundary of the village because it is already clear by the enclosure. The second village precinct is mentioned for the purpose of showing the boundary of the village because it is not clear as an enclosure. In that commentary, if it were said that the first village precinct is for showing the boundary of the forest, it should not be stated that way. It should rather be said, "Having gone out from the threshold, all this is forest." If said thus, the boundary of the forest would be shown much more clearly, and no misconception would occur. When it is said, "a clod-throw of a middle-aged man," this second village precinct itself is called "forest" because the village precinct has been analyzed. If it were said to show the boundary of the forest, it would be unsaid, and there would be a misconception that it is a precinct other than the forest. Was it not said, "This is first stated to determine the precinct of a fenced village"? Although the effort was made to show the boundary of the forest by saying "village precinct" etc., the purpose of saying "a clod-throw of a middle-aged man standing at the threshold" is this: in the Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā), it is stated, "This clod-throw of an unfenced village is the precinct," which means determining the precinct of that unfenced village. How is this known? Because the term "village precinct" (gāmūpacāra) is extracted and shown without extracting the term "forest" (arañña). In that second Pārājika training rule, by extracting the term "village precinct" which is not in the matrix (mātikā), three meanings are shown. They are: one meaning is showing the boundary of the forest; one meaning is showing the boundary together with the precinct of an unfenced village; and one meaning is to be known as the incidental purpose that not only the useful precinct of an unfenced village should be shown in the context of Vinaya, but also the useless precinct of a fenced village can be obtained by this method. The Buddha spoke these words, "a clod-throw of a middle-aged man standing at the house-precinct of an unfenced village," based on three reasons. They are: one meaning is showing the boundary of an unfenced village; one meaning is showing that this first village precinct itself is the precinct in the context of the non-separation boundary (avippavāsa-sīmā); and one meaning is showing that the place where the second clod-throw falls for one standing in that first clod-throw precinct is the functional precinct in all training rules related to towns and villages. Thus, it should be understood that the Buddha, by the power of His omniscience that makes His teaching elegant, extracted each term and showed three meanings for each.
39:
Similarly, in the formal act (kammavācā) for establishing the non-separation boundary (avippavāsa-sīmā), in the passage "excluding the village and the village precinct," the meaning is: if there is a fence for the village, exclude the village; if there is no fence, exclude the village precinct. This method is very appropriate when establishing the non-separation boundary in a monastery (ārāma) located between a fenced village and an unfenced village. By excluding both the village and the village precinct, as per the method mentioned before, one can exclude both the village and the village precinct in both fenced and unfenced villages. It is stated in the Ganthipada: "In the interiors of monasteries, monks who follow the traditional practice establish the non-separation boundary." Some teachers say: "Because the Sekhiya training rules related to the interior of a house cannot occur within a monastery, the monastery interior does not come under the designation of a village; therefore, the non-separation boundary can indeed be established there." The view of those monks should be rejected by showing that the second village precinct has the nature of being designated as a village, and thus this second non-separation kammavācā does not exist for those bhikkhunīs. Although the interior of a monastery is a village, it should be known as an allowable ground (kappiya-bhūmi), like the dwellings of non-Buddhists.

To show the extent of an offense,
And likewise the extent of a non-offense,
In the explanation of the training rules related to the village,
The Such-like One (the Buddha) has shown here both the village and the village precinct.
The boundary (sīmā) and the boundary precinct (sīmūpacāra)
Are not extracted because they are not fixed.
There are two kinds of precincts, by way of external and internal;
There would be four kinds by the division of fenced and unfenced.

This word "precinct" (upacāra) is seen in the sense of an external precinct in the Vinaya Piṭaka in such passages as: "I allow, monks, even one who is not ill to carry a parasol in a monastery and in a monastery precinct." An external precinct means a distance of one clod-throw from the enclosure or from a place suitable for an enclosure. However, in such passages as: "The interior of a monastery (ajjhārāma) means the inside of a fenced monastery, or the precinct of an unfenced monastery; the interior of a dwelling (ajjhāvasatha) means the inside of a fenced dwelling, or the precinct of an unfenced dwelling," the word "precinct" is seen in the sense of an internal precinct. An internal precinct means the enclosure itself or the place suitable for an enclosure. But here, the enclosure is not called "ajjhārāma" or "ajjhāvasatha," nor is it called "inside the monastery" or "inside the dwelling." Among those two kinds of precincts divided into external and internal, in the context of the non-separation boundary, in the passage "excluding the village and the village precinct," the village precinct means...
40:
In this context (regarding the matter of the avippavāsa-sīmā), only the internal vicinity (abbhantarūpacāra) is intended, not the external vicinity (bāhirūpacāra). It should be understood that the internal vicinity is intended for two reasons: because a bhikkhunī has the perception of 'forest' (in the external vicinity), and because that place is where the bhikkhunī would commit the offense of going into the village vicinity (gāmantara-gamana-āpatti). Among those vicinities, it should be understood that in the analysis (vibhaṅga) of this Adinnādāna Pārājika rule, the first village vicinity shown is the external vicinity, and the second vicinity, called 'village', is the internal vicinity. It should be understood that by the description of the vicinity of the first (enclosed) village, the external vicinity called the 'second clod-throw' of an unenclosed village is implied; and by the description of the vicinity of the second (unenclosed) village, which is the village itself, the internal vicinity called 'outside the enclosure' of an enclosed village is indirectly shown. Thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One, through the elegance of His teaching, has shown four types of vicinities in this second Pārājika rule; this method should be carefully noted and applied appropriately after consulting with teachers proficient in the Vinaya. Otherwise—

The ignorant one who would describe this Vinaya,
Not fully understanding the Buddha of great power,
Nor the profound nature of the Dhamma’s methods,
Is dull-sighted and a cause for the destruction of the Dispensation.

He who destroys the Pali, its meaning,
And the methods of the Commentaries, without full understanding,
That ignorant one, though honored by others,
Makes a definitive judgment of 'village' even on those vicinities that should not be so determined.

The ignorant monk, who considers himself wise,
And is honored in succession by the great multitude,
Without resolving the doubts of the unwise,
Displays the graceful manner of a teacher in public.

In that Pārājika Pali, after extracting the definitions: "The vicinity of a village is called village-vicinity; the vicinity called 'village' is called village-vicinity," the text says, "the clod-throw of a medium-sized man standing at the central pillar (indakhīla) of an enclosed village" to show the vicinity of a village. Then, to show the vicinity that is called 'village' itself, it says, "the clod-throw of a medium-sized man standing at the house-vicinity of an unenclosed village." With reference to this meaning, it is written that in the rules such as entering a village at the wrong time (vikāla-gāmapavesana), the village-vicinity (gāmantara), and the agreement on non-separation from robes (avippavāsa-sammuti), only the area worthy of being enclosed is called the 'village' vicinity (for an unenclosed village).
41:
In the phrase "Atthato ekaṃ," the word "saṅkhā" is taken as synonymous with the word "saṅkhāta." The term "ādiyeyya" (should take) is a common term applicable to the twenty-five ways of theft (avahāra). It means taking possession of fields and so forth by moving boundary posts and such through the method of shifting from its place (thānācāvana). In the theft by shifting from its place, just as an offense is committed regardless of whether the owner has abandoned hope (of recovery) or not, the same should be understood in this case of joint effort (sahappayoga) theft.

Because all participants have the same intention, thinking "We shall steal such and such a property," it is stated as "even by one person." If an injunction (āṇatti) is desired, one type of theft called saṃvidhā-vavahāra must be excluded.

In the case of limiting the space (okāsaparikappa), even if one moves an object from its place, it is still protected (from a Pārājika offense) because it is within the designated space. Exceeding the designated space is the criterion. Some say that because it was first taken with an impure mind, even if it is taken now with a pure mind, it still constitutes (a Pārājika); that statement is not good (not appropriate). In this matter, the decision should be taken after consulting the Samantapāsādikā Commentary.

"Uddhāro natthi" means there is no shifting from its place.

Theft is committed by the mere act of drawing a lot because the entire effort has been completed, not because of the accomplishment of the objective (atthasādhaka). In the phrase "uddhāreyeva rakkhati," although the word "eva" makes it clear that there is no protection if the lot is dropped, the phrase "taṃ uddharitvā" etc. is stated to show the meaning by way of the accomplishment of the objective.

It is written: "Because there are many kings such as those who rule the earth and regional kings (padesarāja), the plural 'Rājāno' is used to include them all." Although the plural is used, it should be understood that this refers only to King Bimbisāra. Although "Rājāno" is used generally without specifying any particular king, it means only King Bimbisāra.

In the phrase "pubbappayoga," a dukkaṭa offense is committed during the preliminary effort of clearing the path to steal, provided it is not yet the occasion for a pācittiya; however, in cutting vines and so forth, it is a pācittiya offense. But if one goes and cuts vines growing on top of a pot, a dukkaṭa offense is committed because it is a joint effort (sahappayoga). Regarding a single item, if they consult, "This is very heavy; you hold one side, and I will hold the other," and move it from its place by the effort of both, the offense arises through body, speech, and mind. If interpreted otherwise, theft by one's own hand (sāhatthika) would not be a factor of theft by command (āṇattika)...
42:
It occurs only in a single object. If one arranges by saying, "This object is so heavy; you take it from one side, and I will take it from the other," and they move it from its place through the effort of both, it occurs through body, speech, and mind. It is written in the Vinayagaṇṭhipada that if any other meaning is taken, it would contradict the defined characteristic which states that sāhatthika (theft by one's own hand) is not a factor of āṇattika (theft by command), and āṇattika is not a factor of sāhatthika. The word "pi" is also written in that same Gaṇṭhipada.

For whichever offense there is bodily or vocal origination,
In that sāhatthika-payoga offense, the vocal factor is just like the mind,
The action (kamma) of that offense is not (specially) prescribed.
If the pair of action (kiriya) and non-action (akiriya) etc. occurs, all three actions would occur,
That is not appropriate because it is contradictory (to the Pāḷi),
Only a single bodily action is appropriate.

## The Commentary on the Second Pārājika is finished.

## 3. The Commentary on the Third Pārājika

Just as ñātapariññā (full understanding of the known) is merely knowing the nature of phenomena as "this is form, this is feeling," and tīraṇapariññā (full understanding by investigation) is knowing the nature of phenomena along with the modes of impermanence etc., such as "form is impermanent," so too in this context, because one cannot commit the act of taking life by a single volition (without action), it is said, "one should deprive of life." Because it is stated as a "human being" (manussaviggaha), in order to show it starting from the most subtle physical state by way of beings in the womb, it is said, "starting from the kalala (embryo)." Here, one who deprives of life separates [the being] from the present. In such deprivation, it is not possible to deprive the momentary present (khaṇapaccuppanna); only the continuum present (santatipaccuppanna) or the duration present (addhāpaccuppanna) can be deprived. How? When that effort [to kill] is made, the life-decad (jīvitadasaka) that has received the effort ceases and serves as a condition for a weakened and diminished momentum (of the material continuity). Just as the continuum present ceases after two or three impulsive moments (javana-vāra) have run, and the duration present ceases accordingly, so it serves as a condition. Therefore, the continuum present or the duration present ceases in the interval without reaching the designated time. Thus, because both can be deprived, it is said that one separates (deprives) from the present.

To clarify the meaning spoken by way of conventional usage as "for this meaning" through the ultimate sense, it is stated, "pāṇa (a living being) should be understood," and so on. It is called payoga (effort) because it is associated with volition accompanied by bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti). What is that effort? It is the movement or striking of weapons etc. on the body. This means the falling of a weapon on another's body through volition accompanied by bodily or vocal intimation. "Standing at a distance" means whether one stands far or near.
43:
Striking with a weapon released from the hand is called nissaggiya-payoga (effort by discharge). The word 'tattha' (therein) refers to the nissaggiya-payoga. In the phrase "let anyone die," it is not possible to [specifically] intend among a great multitude of people. Only the one upon whom the arrow falls can have their life ended; it is not possible to end the life of just anyone [unspecified]. 'Āṇāpana' (commanding) is the accomplishment of the intended purpose through volition accompanied by vocal intimation (vacīviññatti). For this very reason, it is taught: "If one wishes to renounce the training but does not make another hear it, the training is not yet renounced." 'Āṇattiniyāmaka' refers to the factors that fulfill the effort of killing caused by command. Only when these factors are not deficient does the effort of command occur, not otherwise. In the context of 'rūpūpahāra' (bringing about a form):

'If a monk, having a corrupt mind, goes near a woman thinking, "Let this woman die because of not obtaining me," he is a killer of that woman.'
'If he goes for the sake of alms, even knowing [she might die], he is not a killer; for he has no desire for that and is equanimous toward her death.'
'Knowing "My wife and mother cannot live because of separation from me," one who separates from them desiring that death is a killer.'
'If he leaves for the sake of ordination etc., even knowing [they might die], he is not a killer; for he has no desire for that and is equanimous toward her death.'

To show that both are the same by expanding the meaning through the division of the word 'hāraka', it is said, "It is both a weapon and a carrier (hāraka)," and so on. By this, the permanent effort (thāvara-payoga) is shown among efforts such as sāhatthika. Although the phrase 'iti cittamano' is extracted, the meaning of the word 'iti' is not yet stated. Even if not stated, by connecting the word 'iti' which comes by way of context, it should be understood that in the phrase 'iti cittasaṅkappo', it will speak only of death, as it is stated as "one having the perception of death, the volition of death, the intention of death." 'Vuttanayena' (in the manner stated) means by way of the six types of effort. In sāhatthika and nissaggiya efforts, sāhatthika-status should be understood as the bodily intimation arising together with the seventh concluding volition (sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā). In āṇattika, however, because vocal intimation occurs together with all seven volitions, the seven sounds become united and reach the state of each single syllable, and by as many...
44:
They make their intention known through syllables; it should be understood as the state of commanding effort (āṇattika-payoga) of the vocal intimation (vacī-viññatti) arising together with the seventh impulsive volition (javana-cetanā) which produces that final syllable.

## The Explanation of the Third Pārājika is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Fourth Pārājika

If it is asked how it is stated in the words of the Buddha, "Thus I know, thus I see," the Commentary explains the phrase beginning with "Thus I know." It is shown that there is no offense for a monk who speaks out of dullness or extreme delusion, simply because of having evil desires. A monk who says, "In the past, I was a Stream-enterer," speaks figuratively. Just as in the passage, "That monk who lives in your monastery is an Arahant," in the training rule as well, "Thus I know" should be understood as being taught not directly but by implication regarding the present.

## The Explanation of the Fourth Pārājika is finished.

Those who kill their mother, those who kill their father, and those who kill an Arahant reach the third Pārājika. Those who defile a nun and the four monks such as Lambī reach only the first Pārājika. If it is asked, "Since this is so, why are there twenty-four Pārājikas?" It should be said that this is not so, because of not understanding the intention (they do exist). For the four types such as the matricide are intended here as unordained persons. Although the four such as Lambī are included in the first Pārājika, they are mentioned separately because they indulge in sexual intercourse in a certain figurative sense.

In this statement, "He does not obtain [communion] with the monks," only this much is said: "communion consisting of the Uposatha and so on." However, in the Vinaya Commentary, it is explained in detail as "the divisions of Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, the recitation of the Pātimokkha, and formal acts of the Saṅgha." In the Pāḷi, it is taught: "Communion means a common formal act, a common recitation, and equality in training." It is prohibited to perform a formal act of the Saṅgha in any of these three ways. The prohibition such as "Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be recited in an assembly where laypeople are sitting" appears only in the context of Pātimokkha and Pavāraṇā. In other such instances, there is no prohibition against performing the remaining acts. The teachers also say, "It is allowable to perform the remaining acts; there is no offense."

It is taught just as for a real monk: "For a monk who charges a monk who has committed an ultimate offense (Pārājika) with a groundless Pārājika, there is a Saṅghādisesa offense. For a monk who charges with a Saṅghādisesa offense, there is a Pācittiya offense." There is no Dukkaṭa offense as there would be for a layperson or a novice. Therefore, the teachers say that sleeping together with that pseudo-monk and accepting offerings from him are allowable for a real monk. The teachers of the Vajirabuddhi say that the phrase "as before, so after" is taught intending only the unfitness for communion, which is taught as "a common formal act, a common recitation, and equality in training." This statement should be investigated.

Now I shall speak of the miscellaneous section pertaining to all four [Pārājikas]. Among those who indulge in sexual intercourse, there is one who has fallen into Pārājika and is not to be associated with.
45:
It is taught that for a monk who charges [another] with a Saṅghādisesa offense, there is a Pācittiya offense, just as it is said for a real monk; it is not a Dukkaṭa as for one who is not ordained. Therefore, the teachers say that sleeping together with that pseudo-monk and accepting offerings from him are allowable for a real monk. The teachers of the Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā say that the phrase "as before, so after" is taught intending only the unfitness for communion, which is taught as "a common formal act, a common recitation, and equality in training." This statement should be investigated and reflected upon.

## Now, the Miscellaneous Section Pertaining to All Four [Pārājikas]:

Among those who indulge in sexual intercourse, there is one who has fallen into Pārājika and is without communion (asaṃvāsa). There is one who has not fallen into Pārājika but is without communion. There is one who has not fallen into Pārājika and has communion, indulging in a matter of Dukkaṭa or Thullaccaya. There is a Pakkhapaṇḍaka (half-month eunuch) who, having been ordained during the non-paṇḍaka period, indulges in sexual intercourse during the paṇḍaka period; he remains without falling into Pārājika. Because that paṇḍaka does not incur an offense, he is not called one who has fallen into Pārājika. This is because there is no such thing as an offense for one who is not a monk. If it is asked whether that paṇḍaka, because he does not incur an offense, becomes one without communion when he returns to the non-paṇḍaka state, the answer is: he does become one without communion. For it is taught, "He is unfit by that physical frame." Because it is taught, "Whatever monk, having reached the training and livelihood of monks... is without communion," only one who indulges in sexual intercourse while being a monk is unfit. If it is argued that this paṇḍaka is not one without communion because he has not fallen into Pārājika, it is not so (he is indeed without communion). Just as in the passage where it is taught, "The Saṅgha should be informed by an experienced and competent monk," where the formal act is successful even if the motion (kammavācā) is recited by a non-monk because there is no failure of the act (kamma-vipatti), this fulfillment should be understood in the same way. Here is the distinction: if a pseudo-monk who was previously ordained recites the motion in this way, and if the Saṅgha perceives him as a real monk, the act is successful; otherwise, the act is not successful—this is our view, says the teacher.

If a layman, a sectarian (titthiya), or a paṇḍaka recites the motion, it is not considered as the motion being recited by the Saṅgha. For it is taught, "The Saṅgha should ordain, the Saṅgha ordains, he has been ordained by the Saṅgha." Therefore, since the motion must be recited by the Saṅgha, it should be understood that it is considered recited by the Saṅgha only when recited by one who belongs to the Saṅgha or one who is perceived as belonging to the Saṅgha (a pseudo-monk who has fallen into Pārājika), and not by any layman, sectarian, paṇḍaka, etc. This same logic should be applied to all formal acts.

Likewise, among those who indulge in sexual intercourse, there is one who should be destroyed (expelled). Because it is taught, "He who defiles a nun, he should be destroyed," that person is indeed...
46:
Such a pseudo-monk causes an offense of sleeping together (sahaseyya) or other such offenses (to other monks). Due to insulting and abusing him, an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) occurs. One who indulges in sexual intercourse with a person who is not a bhikkhunī (such as a sikkhamānā or a sāmaṇerī) should not be expelled from the Sasana (should not be made to disrobe). This is because there is no Pali text spoken by the Buddha stating, "Monks, an unordained person (anupasampanna) who has committed an ultimate matter (antimavatthu/pārājika) should not be ordained." For that very reason, such a person still falls under the designation of 'ordained' (upasampanna); he does not cause offenses such as sleeping together (sahaseyya), and because he is simply one with whom there is no communion (asaṃvāsa), he cannot be one who completes a quorum (gaṇapūraka).

Communion (saṃvāsa) is defined only as performing major and minor ecclesiastical acts together and reciting the Pātimokkha together. Having the same training (sikkhā) to be practiced is also called communion. For that reason, there is no longer communion with that person. However, the appearance of a reason is seen that he causes an offense of teaching Dhamma word by word (padasodhamma). Just as a bhikkhunī is in non-communion (asaṃvāsa) with the Bhikkhu Saṅgha because of the absence of communion such as performing acts together, so too a bhikkhu is in non-communion with a bhikkhunī. However, he does not cause an offense of padasodhamma. Likewise, some who have committed an ultimate matter (antimavatthu) are not included because they are to be ignored along with the shadow of the reason, based on the indication: "It is said that such a person should be expelled."

Furthermore, because of the statement, "Both should be expelled, the corrupter should be expelled," and the statement, "Expel the bhikkhunī Mettiya," it should be understood that even a person who, having entered the midst of the Saṅgha and being investigated by an investigator, is defeated (parājita), is merely an unordained person (anupasampanna). Therefore, he does not cause an offense of expiation involving insulting speech (omasavāda pācittiya).

Moreover, herein, the fourfold classification (catukka) of those who relinquish the training should be understood. There is a person who has relinquished the training but is not endowed with the training and livelihood (sikkhāsājīvasamāpanna). There is a person who has not relinquished the training but is endowed with the training and livelihood. There is a person who has both relinquished the training and is endowed with the training and livelihood. There is a person who has neither relinquished the training nor is endowed with the training and livelihood. Among these four, the third person should be understood as a bhikkhunī who relinquishes the training. The reason is that as long as that bhikkhunī does not give up her marks (liṅga), even if she relinquishes the training while still possessing the effort in the robes and wishing to fall away from the state of a nun, she is still a bhikkhunī and is one endowed with the training and livelihood. For the Blessed One said, "Monks, there is no relinquishing of the training for a bhikkhunī." When does she cease to be a bhikkhunī? She ceases to be a bhikkhunī when she falls under the designation of 'one who has disrobed' (vibbantā). For the Blessed One said, "Only when she has disrobed, then is she no longer a bhikkhunī." To what extent is she called 'disrobed'? Wishing to fall away from the state of a nun, she has no regard for the robes and removes the robes, or goes naked, or goes covered with grass or leaves,
47:
or wears the robes in the manner of a layperson, or wears white clothing, or enters among sectarians (titthiya) while still in her form as a bhikkhunī and undertakes the practices of sectarians such as plucking out hair, or adopts the marks of a sectarian—at that time, she is called 'one who has disrobed' (vibbantā). Among those modes of disrobing, if a bhikkhunī, while still remaining in her own form, undertakes the practices of sectarians, that bhikkhunī, like a monk who has gone over to sectarians, cannot later obtain even the going forth (pabbajjā). Other bhikkhunīs can obtain only the going forth, but cannot obtain higher ordination (upasampadā).

In the Cūḷavagga Pali, according to the statement: "Monks, a bhikkhunī who has gone over from her own residence to a sectarian fold (titthāyatana) should not be ordained upon her return," it seems as if it is permitted that a bhikkhunī who first disrobes and later goes over to a sectarian fold should be ordained upon her return. However, because the Masters of the Council (Saṅgīti-ācariya) have stated, "There are twenty-four Pārājikas," that bhikkhunī should not be ordained again. It is precisely because there is no permission to return to the bhikkhunī state after disrobing that the Blessed One did not allow the relinquishing of the training (sikkhāpaccakkhāna) for bhikkhunīs. A bhikkhunī who has committed an ultimate matter (antimavatthu) and a bhikkhunī who is a pakkhapaṇḍaka are still considered bhikkhunīs (within the context of the fourfold classification). This method should be applied and explained accordingly to all four types of persons.

## Section on Saṅghādisesa
## 1. Explanation of the Training Rule on the Emission of Semen

Regarding the phrase 'except in a dream' (aññatra supinantā), because a dream has a weak physical basis, the volition (cetanā) occurring in a dream is unable to pull the result of rebirth (paṭisandhi). The mental image (nimitta) that appears in a dream is very weak. However, during the course of life (pavatti), it gives results when supported by other wholesome or unwholesome deeds. It is written that even if it gives results, because it arises in a state where one cannot exercise restraint, the volition in a dream is considered negligible (abbohārika).

In this context, the statement 'the mental image that appears in a dream is weak' is not always true. Consciousness is not weak simply because the object is weak, for consciousness is not weak when it takes past or future objects, or when it takes a concept (paññatti) as an object. Therefore, the teacher of the Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā states: 'Our view is that "having a weak physical basis" means "having a weak heart-base (hadaya-vatthu)".' If one asks whether it is appropriate to say it is weak because it lacks a physical basis, the answer is no. This is because appanā consciousness arising from meditation (bhāvanā) possesses extraordinary power even without a physical basis. Consciousness endowed with the power of meditation, though it is merely a mental phenomenon (nāma), can take up the very heavy physical body and transport it to the Brahma world in a single thought-moment. A sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) consciousness similar to that appanā consciousness, even if it is not appanā, can enable the physical body to fly in the sky.

What is the purpose of making such an inference through wisdom here? It is to make it clear to wisdom that such actions are solely the power of consciousness (cittānubhāva). Why? Because one sees the manifestation of special actions such as standing or jumping due to the power of consciousness. Because it is unmixed like ordinary mind-produced matter (cittaja-rūpa) and because it shifts from its place, the teachers speculate three locations for semen: the mouth of the bladder, the waist, and the entire body. It should be regarded like snake venom. Just as there is no fixed location for venom but it appears when the snake looks with anger, so too there is no fixed location for this semen, but we consider that it appears when one makes an effort through the power of lust (rāga), so says the teacher.

If it is said that the phrase 'even if it has not yet descended into the urinary tract' contradicts the phrase 'just by descending,' the commentary states 'if it has shifted from its place,' etc., to explain that meaning. The meaning is: after making an effort with the sexual organ and causing the semen to shift from its place, it is impossible to prevent it from descending into the urinary tract even if one subsequently feels remorse. Even though it cannot be prevented, if one stops it with the desire to stop it, but it cannot be stopped above the urinary tract, it is said 'or if it goes outside.' This is because semen that has shifted from its place...
49:
...semen that has shifted from its place will inevitably descend into the urinary tract; this is the intention of the commentary. Therefore, it should be understood that both the commentary and the Ganthipada views are in agreement.

Here, one might ask: 'Why is the agent (kāraka), such as "whatever monk," not specified in this training rule?' It is answered that the agent is not specified because of the dependence on the intention (adhippāya) for release, and to show that state of dependence. How? For a monk who is motivated by the intention to relieve an itch, etc., or who makes an effort regarding an itch, etc., or who, through the power of sexual lust, makes an effort regarding the thighs and such objects of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa), or regarding sores and such objects of grave offense (thullaccaya)—even if there is emission of semen, it is not a Saṅghādisesa because of the statement: 'There is no offense for a monk who does not intend to emit semen.' Therefore, the agent is not specified here to demonstrate that meaning. Otherwise, if the agent were specified as 'Whatever monk should intentionally reach the emission of semen, it is a Saṅghādisesa,' it would contradict the statement: 'If he intends but does not make an effort and it is emitted, there is no offense.' Likewise, if it were specified in the locative case (sattami) as 'In the intentional emission of semen, except in a dream, it is a Saṅghādisesa,' there would be the same contradiction because of the determination of the causal meaning. Therefore, without using either of those two word orders, it is stated: 'Intentional emission of semen, except in a dream, is a Saṅghādisesa.' In that statement, since the locative case is not used in the sense of a cause (nimitta), the determination of the causal meaning is not made. It should be understood that by not making that determination, the meaning is shown that intentional emission of semen, except in a dream, is a Saṅghādisesa, and that if there is no effort, there is no offense.

In this training rule, two thousand offenses can occur as follows: For a monk who emits blue semen for the sake of health when the sexual organ is functional through the support of lust regarding his own internal body (ajjhatta-rūpa) such as the hand, there is one offense. With the support of lust regarding the internal body, by way of emitting yellow semen and so on, there are nine; thus, there are ten. In this manner, by way of the nine purposes such as 'desiring pleasure,' there are one hundred offenses regarding the internal body when there is the support of lust. Similarly, when there is support from feces, urine, wind, or the bite of an 'uccālinga' insect, if one counts one hundred for each, the total is five hundred. Just as there are five hundred regarding the internal body, so too there are five hundred regarding external bodies (bahiddhā-rūpa), five hundred regarding internal-external bodies, and five hundred for a monk who emits while shaking his waist in the air; thus, it should be known that there are two thousand offenses.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Emission of Semen is finished.
