## 2. Kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

By this word "Otiṇṇo" (overcome), it is shown that the monk has the desire to indulge (in lust for physical contact). For this very reason, it is said, "This is a designation for one possessed by lust for physical contact." By the phrase "Vipariṇatena... saddhiṃ" (with a perverted [mind]... together), his effort (exertion) is shown. The word "saddhiṃ" indicates connection, and that connection is indeed a meeting. With what kind of mind does he meet? It is with a perverted (lustful) mind, and the meaning is that it is not with a mind intending to receive a bowl and so forth. By the phrase "Kāyasaṃsaggāṃ samāpajjeyya" (should engage in physical contact), it amounts to showing the awareness of the touch by that monk who is making an effort. Only a monk who makes an effort and is aware of the touch is said to "engage" in physical contact. In this way, the fulfillment of the three factors of this monk is shown.

Alternatively, a perverted mind is one that has descended into lust, just as a spirit (yakkha) and so forth possesses a being. Or, this instrumental case "vipariṇatena cittena" is used in the sense of the accusative; it is the descending into a perverted mind, just as a being falls into a pit and so forth. Alternatively, even if one has entered the monkhood thinking, "I will be one who has crossed over from lust," because of a mind perverted from that desire to cross over, he descends back into that very lust. This contact occurs either with a woman (mātugāma) who comes to his presence or with a woman to whom he himself goes. In this context, whether the woman is lustful or not lustful is not the measure (not the deciding factor).

In the word "Hatthaggāhaṃ" (taking the hand), the word "hattha" (hand) should be taken to include the entire organic (upādinnaka) body, and not inorganic things like clothes or ornaments which are not continuous with the body. By the term "Veṇiggahaṇa" (taking the braid), it should be understood that inorganic but continuous parts such as hair, body hair, nails, tips of teeth, etc., which are produced by kamma, temperature, and so forth, are included. For this very reason, it is said, "Even for one touching hair with hair (an offense occurs)." Therefore, in this training rule "Aññatarassa vā... parāmasanaṃ," the status of the remaining hair and so forth, which are inorganic, as factors should be understood.

If it is asked, "If this is so, does it not contradict the statement 'Saṅghādisesa for one aware of the touch'?" the answer is: No, it does not, because that meaning is understood. One who recognizes the state of being touched is also called one who is aware of the touch; it is not merely by the arising of body-consciousness. In this context, body-consciousness is inconstant (anekantika). For this very reason, awareness of touch is not stated here as a separate factor. If that awareness of touch were stated as a factor, there would be grounds to think, "Even though hair touched hair, body-consciousness did not arise in me; therefore, I did not perceive the touch," and thus consider it as no offense. It is said, "A braid (veṇī) is often mixed with coins, garlands, and so forth; at that time, if one intends to grab the braid but grabs only the coins, garlands, etc., and not the hair, there is no Saṅghādisesa." This statement should be carefully investigated.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Physical Contact is finished.

## 3. Duṭṭhullavācāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

The request, "When will your mother be pleased?" is spoken for the purpose of showing the characteristic of reaching the peak of lewd speech; it is not spoken for the purpose of showing that lewd speech exists only in words connected to sexual intercourse. The phrase "Ubhatobyañjanakāsi" (You are a hermaphrodite), however, is speech mixed with the male organ, which is a case where Saṅghādisesa does not apply. In a male hermaphrodite, the female organ is hidden and the other, the male organ, is prominent. Some teachers say, "If that speech also causes a Saṅghādisesa offense, then why do terms like 'animittāsi' (you are organ-less) and so forth not cause a Saṅghādisesa offense?" That statement is not proper, both because it is a designation for a male organ and because the characteristic for the offense has been taught in the Matika as "Saṅghādisesa for words connected to sexual intercourse."

In speaking lewdly with words connected to sexual intercourse, if the woman understands, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense; if she does not understand, it is a Thullaccaya offense. In speaking with other words, if she understands, it is a Thullaccaya offense; if she does not understand, it is a Dukkaṭa offense—so say some teachers. This matter should be taken after careful investigation. In this training rule, it may be asked: "Why is it said to have 'two feelings' (pleasant and neutral) instead of 'three feelings,' since anger arises in one who insults with words like 'Sikharani' and so forth?" This offense occurs by the power of lust, not by the power of anger. Therefore, only an insult proceeding by the power of lust is intended here. Thus, the statement "two feelings" is indeed well-spoken.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Lewd Words is finished.

## 4. Attakāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In speaking lewd words, if one speaks to a woman of the aforementioned type (who is capable of understanding lewd and non-lewd speech) praising the merit of serving with the sexual act that one desires for the sake of another monk, it is a Dukkaṭa offense. If one speaks indirectly, saying, "Whichever monk lives in your monastery, give to him the highest gift, the practice of sexual intercourse," it is also a Dukkaṭa offense. Some teachers say this is because it is stated, "One should praise the merit of serving with the sexual act that one desires, to one of virtue like me." Others say it is a Saṅghādisesa offense because of the presence of the five factors. This decision should be taken after investigation. It is written, "In these two training rules, as in the case of physical contact, it is said that a Thullaccaya offense is incurred for lewd words or words for serving with the sexual act spoken to female spirits (yakkhi) or female ghosts (peti). However, this does not appear directly in the Commentaries." A hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka) is of the same class as a pandaka (paṇḍaka).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Serving One's Own Lusts is finished.

## 5. Sañcarittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

*Alaṃvacanīyā* refers to a woman who is not a permanent wife and should not be spoken to or solicited. The word *alaṃ* is used in the sense of prohibition. That which is not *alaṃvacanīyā* (meaning, a woman who can be spoken to or solicited) is called *nālaṃvacanīyā*. It is stated in the Pārājika Pali: "He accepts, inquires, and reports back; there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*." Therefore, for a monk acting as a go-between, a *saṅghādisesa* offense definitely occurs. It is written that teachers say there are no *dukkaṭa* or *thullaccaya* offenses arising from the preliminary efforts of accepting or inquiring for such a monk.

In this training rule, although the *Padabhājanī* Pali does not explicitly state, "A woman means a human woman, not a female yakkha, a female peta, or a female animal; a man means a human man, not a male yakkha, a male peta, or a male animal," it is clear that it refers only to a human woman because in training rules such as *Kāyasaṃsarga* (physical contact), the definition of a woman is given as "A woman (*mātugāma*) means a human woman." Since the preliminary actions for sexual intercourse are similar, by defining the woman, the definition of the man is also completed. For this very reason, it was said in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-aṭṭhakathā*: "Those for whom one acts as a go-between are of human birth."

Just as in the training rules like *Kāyasaṃsarga*, where *paṇḍakas*, female *yakkhas*, and female *petas* are mentioned as bases for a *thullaccaya* offense, the same applies here. Because of having the nature of a *paṇḍaka*, a human *ubhatobyañjanaka* (hermaphrodite) is also a base for a *thullaccaya* offense. It should be understood that others, such as human men with each other, *paṇḍakas* who are *yakkhas*, *ubhatobyañjanakas*, and male animals, are only bases for *dukkaṭa* offenses, as they have the nature of being seen as sexual misconduct (*micchācāra*).

## The Explanation of the Sañcaritta Training Rule is Finished.

## 6. Kuṭikārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

When asked even this much, "What is it, Bhante?", the monk who is asked is allowed to solicit for the purpose of the manual labor for which he entered. It is written that this is because he was asked while performing the duties of a monk on alms-round.

If a lay supporter who is asked for manual labor expects, "He will give the materials or the cost," and the monk solicits the labor, is it allowable or not? Some teachers say it is allowable because it is obtained through intimation (*obhāsaparikathā*) regarding the lodging.

In the phrase "measuring three cubits," it refers to three cubits by a carpenter's cubit. "A couch of standard measurement" refers to a couch that is nine spans by the standard span. It is written that if that couch cannot be turned this way or that in a small hut, or if the hut is not four cubits in width, it does not count as a *kuṭī* (hut) and is therefore allowable.

Furthermore, for a small hut that does not fall under the category of a *kuṭī*, there is no duty to have the site designated, as it is taught that plastering may be done.

"Plastering inside and out... refers only to the roof"—this statement is appropriate. Why? Because
53:
It is written that for a monk who has a wall made of smooth clay erected and then plasters the top, the inside, the outside, or both, in connection with the wall, an offense occurs even if there is no plastering on the wall itself. If it is taken this way (as referring only to the roof), then the pillars, beams, door-frames, etc., would be useless. Therefore, this statement should be accepted only after careful scrutiny. If a monk builds with the thought, "This will also be an Uposatha hall, and I will also live there," or "I will live together with monks or novices," it is indeed allowable. Why? It is written that this is because it was taught as "for one's own use" (*attuddesa*).

This training rule, like the fourth *Pārājika* training rule, depends on the origin (*nidāna*). The monks living on the banks of the Vaggumudā River did not themselves speak of superior human states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) that they did not possess in a way that constitutes the characteristic of false speech (*musāvāda*). They only spoke of each other's superior human states. Although a *Pārājika* case does not occur merely by such speaking, the Blessed One, based on that much of an indication, made that story the origin and laid down the *Pārājika* offense. The same applies here. In this origin, it was not said, "A site not designated, with danger, without a perimeter." However, because it was said, "of improper measurement," for one who exceeds the measurement, it is only a *saṅghādisesa* offense that depends on the origin. Although in that *kuṭī-kāra* (hut-building) it appears as if it involves *saṅghādisesa* regarding danger (*sārambha*) and lack of perimeter (*aparikkamana*), it is not prohibited in the *Vibhaṅga* because it is said, "The Vibhaṅga is the regulator of that." The same applies to the *Mahallakavihāra* training rule.

Here, a question arises: For what purpose is the basis for a *dukkaṭa* offense mentioned in the *Mātikā*? Should it not be mentioned only in the *Vibhaṅga*? This is true. Should monks not be led for the designation of the site? The site must be designated by those monks. What kind of site should be designated? One that is without danger (*anārambha*) and has a perimeter (*saparikkamana*). The other type, involving danger and lack of perimeter, is mentioned because it follows accordingly as, "If a monk (builds) on a site with danger and without a perimeter." Since a site (*vatthu*) can be of many kinds—with danger and without perimeter, without danger and with perimeter, with danger and with perimeter, without danger and without perimeter—it is meant that because of these many kinds, only a site without danger and with a perimeter should be designated, and not any other.

If it is asked, "What is the benefit of designating the site here?", it is because it is a means of avoiding the cause for laying down a heavy offense (*garukāpatti*). Indeed, the non-designation of the site is the root cause for laying down a heavy offense. The laying down of a heavy offense causes harassment to laypeople through improper verbal intimation (*vacīviññatti*). There is also the state of danger which is a cause of suffering for oneself and suffering for others. These sufferings and dangers are avoided by the means of designating the site. Monks do not designate a site for the purpose of harassing laypeople to build an unallowable hut, or for the purpose of building a hut on a site with danger. In this regard, there are these verses:
54:
The manifestation of the bases of the dukkaṭa offenses in the training rule has been made;
The causes for the occurrence of those grave offenses (garukāpatti) have thus been manifested.
Because the causes of grave offenses are avoided by the method of pointing out the site for the hut,
Therefore, impetuosity (sārambha) and so forth have been abandoned.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Hut-building (Kuṭikāra-sikkhāpada) is finished.

## 7. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Dwelling-building (Vihārakāra-sikkhāpada)

This training rule on dwelling-building is only of the nature of non-action (akiriya), because an offense is incurred merely by not performing [the required action]. This occurs through the failure to have the site for the hut pointed out. In the phrase "bhikkhū vā anabhineyya," the word "vā" should be understood as having a restrictive meaning. Since it is stated, "The venerable Channa had a shrine-tree cut down," this training rule should also be understood as being dependent on the origin (nidāna).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Dwelling-building is finished.

## 8. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Corrupt Malice (Duṭṭhadosa-sikkhāpada)

Because it is said, "Why do you not perform salutation and so forth to me? ... the head comes only when joined," some say that it is not proper to salute a monk who has reached the ultimate case (i.e., one who has committed a pārājika offense); that statement should not be accepted. This is because it is not mentioned in the Pali text starting with "How many, venerable sir, are those not to be saluted?" in the Upālipañcaka at the end of the Parivāra, and because it is stated, "One who is later ordained should salute one who was earlier ordained." Therefore, in this Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī commentary, it is said, "Ordained (upasampanna) means reaching the status of a monk." The intention of the Sutta should be taken as follows: it is said for the purpose of showing that a monk who does not salute is said to accuse with an accusation characterized by the rejection of proper conduct (sāmīci). For that very reason, it is said, "By this much, it is called an accusation." To show the manner of incurring the offense intended in this training rule, it is written, "Why do you not perform salutation and so forth to me?" and so on.

"Katūpasampada" refers to the person for whom the higher ordination is successful (such as eunuchs and so forth). In the term "ṭhapanakkhetta," the suspension of the Pavāraṇā is of two kinds: the universal suspension (sabbasaṅgāhika) and the individual suspension (puggalika).
55:
Among those two kinds of suspension of the Pavāraṇā, in the universal suspension (sabbasaṅgāhika), it is from the syllable "su" to the syllable "re" in the formula "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sir... I invite [the Saṅgha] for the third time (tevācikaṃ pavāre)." In the individual suspension (puggalika), it is from the syllable "saṃ" to this final syllable "ṭi" in the formula "Venerable sir, I invite the Saṅgha... seeing, I [shall] perform (passanto paṭi) [the remedy]." A monk who suspends even a single word within this interval has suspended the Pavāraṇā. Furthermore, in the suspension of the Uposatha ceremony, the distinction should be understood according to this same method, not exceeding the syllable "re" in the final word "kareyya."

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Corrupt Malice is finished.

## 9. The Explanation of the Training Rule on a Different Category (Aññabhāgiya-sikkhāpada)

"Aññabhāgo vā assa atthi" (or he has a different portion) is like saying "sovaṇṇa" because it is the property of gold, or "suvaṇṇa" because it has a beautiful color. In calling that he-goat "aññabhāgiya," the body of an image, the body of a stone statue, etc., are examples. The name "Dabba" given to the he-goat is called "desa" (a part/point). Why is it called "desa"? Because for the purpose of accusing the Elder Dabba, the name of the Elder can also be pointed out. It adheres not only to the Elder Dabba but also to another object, the he-goat. It is called "lesa" (a pretext) because it adheres slightly only by way of common usage and not by way of actual substance. The root "lis" is used in the sense of adhering only by name to the mountain goat other than the Elder Dabba. Therefore, it is said, "It is called lesa because it adheres slightly." Since the terms "desa" and "lesa" do not differ in meaning, the word "kiñci desaṃ lesamattaṃ upādāya" (taking some point or a mere pretext) is extracted and taught in the Padabhājanī as "The ten pretexts, the pretext of birth (jātilesa)," and so forth.

In the phrase "aṭṭhuppattivasena eva āvibhūtaṃ" (manifested only by way of the occurrence of the matter), it is not analyzed because there is no fixed rule in another way. Why? Because for all other monks, unlike the Mettiya and Bhummajaka monks, it is not only a goat that is the subject of a different category (aññabhāgiya); other animals like cows, buffaloes, etc., can also be the subject. Furthermore, not all monks, like the Mettiya and Bhummajaka monks, take only a mere hint of a name; they also take other hints such as birth (jāti) and so forth. Therefore, because there is no constant rule, it is not analyzed. Again, if it were said so, the status of being a different category would be possible only for the goat and not for others, as if only that goat were shown. And the pretext (lesa) would be only the pretext of name (nāmalesa) and not birth and so forth, as if only that were shown. It should be understood that it is not analyzed because there is a possibility of such wrong grasping. The phrase "idha ca... saññino pi" means "both in this Aññabhāgiya training rule and in the Amūlaka training rule."
56:
That monk who does not practice the Aññabhāgiya training rule in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma,
He would only reach the state of being one who has a different portion (aññabhāgiyatā) among those who know the Vinaya.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on a Different Category is finished.

## 11. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Following a Schismatic (Bhedānuvattaka-sikkhāpada)

In the passage "They are not worthy of the [legal] act beyond three... they perform," it is written that it is not proper to perform the act by saying (without mentioning the specific names), "These four monks," or "This monk and this monk."

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Following a Schismatic is finished.

## 12. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Difficult to Speak to (Dubbaca-sikkhāpada)

He is called "dubbaca" because he is spoken to with difficulty. When spoken to (by his fellow monks), he does not endure it.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Difficult to Speak to is finished.

## The Explanation of the Conclusion (Nigamana-vaṇṇanā)

There is the reading "nāmamattavasena." It is written as "nāmagottavasena." The meaning is this: if one knows, "This action is not proper for monks to do," and yet conceals it, it is indeed concealed. "Sabhāgamattam eva" means merely being a person of similar nature who is not an enemy.

In the phrase "vatthu ceva gottañca," "vatthu" means the transgression, the emission of semen. "Gotta" is called so because it protects knowledge (gaṃ); it means protecting knowledge and speech without allowing them to go elsewhere from their own class (sajāti). The object (vatthu) goes only to its own class. Here, "sajāti" means an action that is distinct from others like bodily contact (kāyasaṃsagga), etc.; it is not bodily contact and so forth. In the phrase "nāmañceva āpatti ca," "āpatti" means the name of the offense incurred through transgression.
57:
Furthermore, regarding the procedure for informing (ārocana) the monks who arrive, it should be understood as follows: when informing two monks, one should say, 'Venerable sirs, please take note'; when informing three or more monks, one should say, 'Venerable sirs, please take note' (or if there are many monks, 'May the Saṅgha take note').

In the phrase 'without committing a breach of duty (vattabheda) or an interruption of the night (ratticcheda),' a breach of duty occurs in such instances as: accepting the salutation, etc., of monks undergoing penance, such as those deserving to be sent back to the beginning (mūlāya paṭikassana), excluding a fellow probationer (pārivāsika) who is junior to oneself; sitting in order of seniority; exhorting bhikkhunīs; and criticizing monks who perform legal acts (kammika). An interruption of the night occurs in such instances as: failing to inform monks who are within the range of sight or hearing; living under the same roof with a regular monk (pakatatta); and monks arriving at or leaving the monastery without one's knowledge.

Since Vinaya acts cannot be performed with monks of a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka), there is no interruption of the night even if one does not inform them. Based on the statement 'beyond the distance of two stone-throws,' it is not proper to undertake the duty within the precinct (upacāra). A monk who has laid down the duty (nikkhittavatta), if he had previously undertaken and informed a certain monk, must also inform that same monk when laying down the duty later. Therefore, if that monk departs at the time of re-undertaking the duty, even if one has informed him during the day without him arriving on that day, if the day has passed, it is stated: 'When the dawn rises, one must inform that monk and lay down the duty before going to the monastery.' Furthermore, it is stated: 'Having gone to the monastery, one must inform the first monk one sees and then lay down the duty.' If an interruption of the night occurs, one would have to inform all the monks within the boundary (sīmā) of the monastery. This statement 'having informed that monk' is said for the purpose of protecting against a breach of duty, referring to a monk who was not informed previously. For this very reason, it is stated in the Samantapāsādikā: 'another monk who is either leaving the monastery or arriving.'

In the case of Suddhanta-parivāsa (absolute probation), if one has taken it thinking, 'I have been impure for about a month,' and while undergoing probation, one later decides on a shorter or longer period, one must undergo probation for that entire period; there is no need for a new granting of probation. This Suddhanta-parivāsa has the nature of being able to increase upwards or decrease downwards. This is its characteristic.

'Samodahitvā' means including or collecting into the base of the original offense. If an intermediate offense (antarāpatti) is an unconcealed offense, one should undergo it with the previously taken probation without being sent back to the beginning (mūlāya paṭikassana). A monk who, having committed an offense, disrobes and then again...
58:
...becomes ordained and then conceals it; or one who concealed it before but does not conceal it later; or one who conceals it in both periods—to all such monks, Samodhāna-parivāsa (combined probation) should be given according to the number of days concealed. Because it is stated in the Cullavagga Pali, 'either in the former group of offenses' or 'in the latter group of offenses,' two monks may reach a light offense (lahukāpatti) from a Saṅghādisesa offense. They hold the view that they are purified from the Saṅghādisesa offense. One conceals it, while the other does not. The one who conceals it should be made to confess a Dukkaṭa offense. According to the word 'Both should be dealt with according to the Dhamma,' it should be understood that concealing any offense results in a Dukkaṭa offense.

Whether those companion monks go or do not go, one should proceed according to the previous method. In this context, practicing in a group of fewer than four (ūne gaṇe), not rising from an offense, and being separated from the group for even one night—these can occur in both Parivāsa and Mānatta if one leaves for some business before dawn while the Saṅgha is present for even a moment of the night. It is stated in the Samantapāsādikā: 'Because this monk undergoing Mānatta informed the group and stayed while noting the presence of the monks, there is no fault of practicing in a depleted group or being separated.' Therefore, if that monk goes after sitting for even a moment after informing, there is no fault of separation. The living of a probationer (pārivāsika) or an expelled person (ukkhittaka) with a regular monk is prohibited by the distance of the eaves-drop (udakapāta). Therefore, even if the precincts are different, living under the same roof is not proper.

Now, the textual analysis (pāṭhavicāraṇā) should be understood: 'The nine offenses involving the first stage (paṭhamāpattika) and the four involving the third stage (yāvatatiyaka)'—this statement is a natural limitation. By this, it shows that the rising from an offense (vuṭṭhāna) is not fixed. It means that while rising from some offenses occurs through a formal act (kamma) or without a formal act, it is not the same for the commission of an offense. The phrase 'any one or any other' (aññataraṃ vā aññataraṃ vā) indicates that although they are divided into two types, there is no difference in the sequence of rising from the offense. In the phrase 'for as many days, for that many days' (yāvatīhaṃ, tāvatīhaṃ), the determination of days is by means of dawn. By the word 'knowing' (jānaṃ), it shows that a monk who conceals while knowing must undergo probation even against his will (akāmā). 'That monk must undergo probation even against his will' is said to show that the monk undergoing probation must do so even if he does not wish to, and that he is not one whose gender has changed (liṅgaparivattana). In the phrase 'by one who has completed probation' (parivutthaparivāsena), etc., only a monk who has completed probation must practice for six nights as a monk from the beginning, according to the number of days the offense was concealed, for the sake of Mānatta which is higher than probation. A monk whose gender has changed must also practice the six nights of the higher Mānatta for the sake of the monks' esteem. He is not like one in probation who does not have to practice Mānatta due to gender change. Only one who has completed Mānatta should be rehabilitated (abbhetabba), not any other. It shows that even if one is deserving of Mānatta as in probation, or if there is a gender change of a bhikkhunī practicing Pakkha-mānatta, he is not yet a monk who has completed Mānatta. Only after taking the monk's Mānatta again and practicing for six nights should that monk be rehabilitated.
59:
If the gender of a Bhikkhunī who is practicing Pakkhamānatta changes (i.e., she becomes a monk), she becomes a monk who has already practiced Mānatta. It is shown that after undertaking the monk's Mānatta and practicing it for six nights, that monk who has practiced Mānatta should be rehabilitated (Abbhāna).

"Yattha siyā" means in whichever Samānasamvāsaka-sīmā there is a Bhikkhu Saṅgha consisting of a group of twenty. If it is deficient by even one, it is not appropriate to call it a "group of twenty." This is because if the Saṅgha is deficient by even one, it is not a group of twenty. Therefore, one might ask: "Should it not be said simply as 'if the Saṅgha is deficient by even one'?" No, because it serves the purpose of preventing confusion with groups of four (Catuvagga), five (Pañcavagga), or ten (Dasavagga). Therefore, if a Bhikkhu Saṅgha of twenty is deficient by even one monk, the formal act (kamma) should be regarded as failed.

Some monks who are not proficient in the Vinaya might think: "Just as a Saṅgha of more than four is called a 'Catuvagga' in a formal act to be performed by a group of four, so too a Saṅgha of more than five or ten is called a 'Pañcavagga' or 'Dasavagga'. Therefore, even if deficient, it is still a Catuvagga, Pañcavagga, Dasavagga, or Vīsativagga Saṅgha." To prevent their misunderstanding, the phrase "ekenapi ce ūno" (if deficient by even one) and so on was stated. Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as: in a Bhikkhu Saṅgha of twenty, if one monk is excluded and that monk is not a Pakatatta (a monk in good standing, e.g., one undergoing Parivāsa), or if excluding him, it is deficient by one other Pakatatta monk.

The phrase "Ayaṃ tattha sāmīcī" is stated to clarify what was said in all cases of Parivāsa, Mānatta, and Abbhāna: "He gives Parivāsa for that offense, performs Mūlāya Paṭikassanā, gives Mānatta, and rehabilitates (abbheti)." Therefore, it should be understood that in these Saṅghādisesa rules, this stated practice is mandatory; it is not optional as in the Rāja-sikkhāpada and others. In those Rāja-sikkhāpada and similar rules, it is shown that there is no offense if one cannot perform that practice due to some danger.

## The Explanation of Saṅghādisesa is finished.

## Section on the Undetermined Offenses (Aniyata-kaṇḍa)
## 1. Explanation of the First Undetermined Training Rule
At the very beginning of the Aniyata training rules, this miscellaneous note (pakiṇṇaka) is stated. If it is argued: "This Aniyata section is useless because it contains no new offenses (not found in other sections)," the answer is: No, it is useful because it explains the sequence and characteristics of charging or not charging an offense, distinguished by heavy (garuka) and light (lahuka) offenses.

In this Aniyata section, the sequence and characteristics of charging heavy and light offenses are shown by such phrases as: "If that laywoman (upāsikā) should say... and that monk acknowledges it, he should be dealt with according to the offense." The sequence and characteristics of not charging are shown by the phrase: "He should not be dealt with." If it is asked whether these characteristics should be recited at the beginning or the end (of the Pātimokkha), the answer is: No, because it is not possible. Why is it not possible at the beginning? Because the training rules to which these characteristics apply have not yet been shown. Why not at the end? Because it would be mixed only with heavy offenses. Therefore, since it is mixed with both, it deserves to be recited only in the middle of the heavy and light training rules.

In that Aniyata section, the light offense called Pācittiya is shown, and that offense is also called a heavy offense. Therefore, it is said: "By taking delight in privacy, which is called a defilement connected with sexual intercourse," and so on. For this reason, some teachers say it is shown immediately after the heavy training rules. If so, one might ask: "Since the explanation of characteristics is completed by the first Aniyata, what is the use of the second Aniyata?" The answer is: No, it is useful for preventing wrong graspings caused by the specification of the location.

Because the location is specified as "in a screened seat, suitable for sexual intercourse," a wrong grasping might occur that these characteristics do not apply to a location that is the opposite of that. To prevent such wrong grasping, the second Aniyata is also meaningful. Why? Because of the difference in location, the explanation of the different types of privacy, and the explanation of the different types of delighting in sitting in privacy. Due to the specification of the location, the different types of delighting in sitting in privacy arise. Similarly, by showing the different types of physical contact (kāyasaṃsagga), the distinction between the two Rahonisajja training rules can be known. Even in a place not suitable for sexual intercourse and not screened, or in a screened place, physical contact can occur by touching the hair, etc., of a sitting woman that comes out through windows, door cracks, and so on; such methods should be understood in detail.

The following is just a brief illustration regarding the location and so on: "Because of the difference in location" means because of the difference between a place suitable for sexual intercourse and one not suitable. For even some screened places are not suitable for sexual intercourse due to windows, etc...
61:
Due to being obstructed, some concealed places are also unsuitable for sexual intercourse because they are separated by windows and so forth. Some places that are concealed on both sides are also unsuitable for sexual intercourse because they are like an open space for those who can see. In this context, regarding the phrase "raho-bheda-dīpanato" (showing the distinction of seclusion), although the general nature of being in seclusion is the same, the meaning is that seclusion is of two kinds: concealed and unconcealed. "Raho-nisajja-assāda-bheda-dīpanato" (showing the distinction of the enjoyment of sitting in seclusion) means showing such distinctions as sitting by way of enjoying sexual intercourse and sitting by way of enjoying lewd speech.

Some say, "Since this method has already appeared in the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha, it should be understood that this Aniyata section is omitted in the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha." Although some say, "It is omitted because the originating incident (atthuppatti) did not arise in the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha," that statement is improper because it shows an inconsistent nature.

Indeed, in the time of all Buddhas, there are five recitations (uddesa) for monks and four for nuns. Some say this section is omitted because the Saṅghādisesa and Pācittiya offences are not common (asādhāraṇa) in the prescription of the Pātimokkha recitation. In detail, for those nuns, the specific bodily contact by way of the Ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalika training rule and the Aṭṭhavatthuka training rule is a Pārājika matter. By the words "she might consent to the grabbing of the hand, or she might lean her body for that purpose," consenting is also a Pārājika matter; by the words "she might stand," standing is also a Pārājika matter; by the words "she might go to an appointment," going is also a Pārājika matter; and by the words "she might enter a concealed place," entering a concealed place is also a Pārājika matter. Furthermore, by the words "in the darkness of the night without a lamp, in a concealed place or in an open space, she might stand or talk one-on-one," lewd speech is also a Pācittiya matter. Therefore, those teachers consider that the Aniyata section is not separately taught for those nuns because their circumstances differ from those of the monks. This is a miscellaneous discussion.

Since it is stated that "alajjī (shameless) ones and others will accuse the lajjī (shameful) ones by way of offences leading to rehabilitation (desanāvuṭṭhānagāminī)," for the sake of supporting the lajjī monks, a decision should not be made solely by the word of a suitable laywoman (upāsikā), but should be made only by the monk's own confession. As for the offences, they are prescribed to show the defining characteristics for judgment. It is written that one should speak by taking only the detailed method because it shows the recitation: "Venerable sirs, these two are the undetermined (Aniyata) rules."

In the phrase "sotassa raho" (seclusion of the ear), the word "raho" is spoken in a general sense. This is like the word "Pārājika" being associated in a general sense with lewdness in the training rules on announcing lewdness and concealing lewdness. Therefore, it is said, "In this context, only the seclusion of the eye (cakkhusseva raho) is intended." How is this known? Because it is stated, "A woman means... even a girl born that very day," it is already made clear that lewd speech (seclusion of the ear) is not intended here.
62:
In the passage "anto-dvādasa-hatthe pi" (even within twelve cubits), by the word "pi" (also), it means even one sitting at the door of a room with an unclosed door-leaf [does not count as a witness]. In accordance with the passage on non-offence in the Raho-paṭicchannāsana training rule of the Acelaka Chapter, which states "any wise man is the second [person]," it is said, "The presence of even a hundred women does not indeed create a state of non-offence."

In this first Aniyata training rule, "enjoyment of sitting in seclusion" (raho-nisajja-assāda) refers only to the defilement associated with sexual intercourse, because in the Word-for-Word Analysis (Vibhaṅga), it is taught that "suitable for the act" (alaṅkammaniye) means being able to engage in sexual intercourse. It is not the defilement of enjoying lewd speech as in the second [Aniyata rule]. For that reason also, it is clear that the seclusion of the ear is not intended.

Regarding the words "he might be told by one of the three rules," this is spoken for the sake of showing the distinction of Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa offences, rather than stating only a Pācittiya offence, in accordance with that training rule for a monk sitting by way of the Raho-nisajja training rule. Why is the confession of the incident (vatthu) mentioned as "the monk confessing to the sitting," instead of mentioning the confession of the offence? It is said in reply—when accused of an offence and asked by a Vinaya-holder, "Regarding what incident?", and the accused monk replies, "Regarding this incident," and the Vinaya-holder investigates, "Did you do such a thing?", the monk should be made to deal with the offence only when he confesses to the incident; it is for the sake of showing this that "the monk confessing to the sitting" is spoken.

If this is so, should he be made to deal with the offence even if he confesses to the sitting but not the incident? That is indeed appropriate. However, it should be understood in this way: without taking the incidents of the three offences, only the sitting is mentioned here by way of the training rule. This is because if that sitting is accepted, the offences such as Pārājika are already accepted. In the passage "yena vā sā," the word "vā" (or) should be connected as "tena so bhikkhu kāretabbo vā" (by that, that monk should be made to [confess] or...). That word "vā" has the sense of an alternative (vikappa). Therefore, the meaning is: "If he confesses, he should be made to deal [with the offence]; if he does not confess, he should not be made to deal [with it]." Thus, it is stated in the Commentary, "or confessing," and so forth. Since the offences are spoken of as being caused by sitting by way of the Raho-nisajja training rule, in other cases also, the offence should be taken by way of the remaining training rules. Since it is stated in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary that "the origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are just like the first Pārājika," it should be understood that lewd speech is not intended in this first Aniyata training rule.

## The Explanation of the First Aniyata Training Rule is Finished.

## 2. Dutiya-aniyata-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

'Saṅghādisesena vā' means by physical contact or by speaking lewd words. For this very reason, this section on physical contact (kāyasaṃsaggavāra) has also been taught in the Pāḷi. 'Anandho abadhiro' means a person who is not blind sees the physical contact, and a person who is not deaf hears the lewd words; for this very reason, it was written in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) that 'it is just like theft (adinnādāna).'

In this context, if it is asked how the origination (samuṭṭhāna) occurs through body, speech, and mind: Indeed, a monk who engages in physical contact also speaks lewd words, and a monk who speaks lewd words also sits; thus such an origination is possible. Or, it is stated specifically with reference to lewd words. Truly, those lewd words have the same origination as theft.

If a person is like the All-Knowing Buddha, having a mind that enters into understanding the Dhamma teaching which is diverse and distinguished by various methods and aspects, and is mindful, such a person no longer performs that merit which is a cause for gain.
