## Nissaggiya Section
## 1. Robe Chapter (Cīvaravagga)
## 1. Commentary on the Kathina Training Rule

In the Nissaggiya section, the three Kathina training rules, the Rain-cloth training rule (Vassikasāṭika), the Extra-robe training rule (Accekacīvara), and the Suspicious-robe training rule (Sāsaṅka) should be understood as a collection of offenses mixed in various ways in a single teaching.

One should understand the Kathina, the four types of persons (those for whom the Kathina is or is not spread),
The fifteen factors associated with the Kathina,
The two times: the Kathina-spreading time and the Robe time,
And the offenses and partial decisions of the six training rules.

In that verse, 'Kathina' refers to the collection of factors such as the appreciation (anumodanā) of the Saṅgha, the appreciation of the group (gaṇa), and the spreading (atthāra) by an individual, by which the Kathina is considered spread for the Saṅgha, according to the definition. As it is taught: 'Kathina should be known; the collection or combination of those factors is the name.' Therefore, Kathina is merely a name for many factors and is not a single factor in terms of ultimate reality (paramattha). What then is the 'spreading' (atthāra) of that Kathina? It is just a part of that Kathina, like a stream of milk. As it is taught: 'Spreading is included as one factor by way of vocal expression (vacībheda).'

The associated factors (sahajā) are these fifteen: the 8 grounds (mātikā), the 2 obstacles (palibodha), and the 5 benefits (ānisaṃsa). The two times (samayadvaya) are the Kathina-spreading time and the Robe time. Among them, the Kathina-spreading time is the last month of the rainy season. The Robe time is this single month of Kattika if the Kathina is not spread, and if it is spread, it is five months including the four months of winter.

Among them, the 8 grounds (mātikā) are those beginning with 'departure' (pakkamanantikā). All those grounds arise simultaneously with the spreading. This is because the removal (uddhāra) of the Kathina is possible only when there is a spreading. Among those 8 grounds for removal, the 'removal during the interval' (antarubbhāra) and 'simultaneous removal' (sahubbhāra) have simultaneous arising and simultaneous ceasing (ekuppāda ekanirodha) with the spreading. The remaining six grounds for removal have simultaneous arising but different ceasing (ekuppāda nānānirodha). In that context, 'simultaneous ceasing' (ekanirodha) means ceasing along with the spreading; the meaning is that the nature of removal for antarubbhāra and sahubbhāra occurs in a single moment. The others are said to cease separately. Even when those grounds reach the state of removal, the spreading remains as it was—this is the explanation of the meaning in the Commentary. If a monk who has spread the Kathina...
65:
For a monk who departs from a monastery while still having concern for it, if the Saṅgha removes the Kathina by a formal act in the interim (before the full moon of Phagguna), even though the impediment of robes (cīvara-palibodha) consisting of the completion of robes did not initially exist at the original monastery, the impediment is severed upon the interim removal of the Kathina because of his lingering concern and continued effort. In this way, the removal of the Kathina ending with departure (pakkamanantika-kathinuddhāra) is such that its arising is identical to the spreading of the Kathina, but its cessation is different.

Similarly, when there is an interim removal, for a monk who hears of it, as long as the robes are not finished, the removal ending with completion (niṭṭhānantika) occurs because protection remains possible. As long as a decision has not been made, it is the removal ending with decision (sanniṭṭhānantika). As long as the robe is not lost, it is the removal ending with loss (nāsanantika). As long as he has not heard [of the removal], it is the removal ending with hearing (savanantika). As long as the expectation for the robe is not cut off, it is the removal ending with the cutting off of expectation (āsāvacchedika). As long as he has not crossed the boundary, it is the removal ending with the crossing of the boundary (sīmātikkantika). It should be understood that in these cases, the arising is identical to the spreading, but the cessation is different.

Among those removals of the Kathina, the two types—interim removal (antarubbhāra) and simultaneous removal (sahubbhāra)—occur only within the boundary (sīmā), not outside the boundary. Removal ending with departure (pakkamanantika), removal ending with hearing (savanantika), and removal ending with crossing the boundary (sīmātikkantika) occur only outside the boundary, not within it. Removal ending with completion (niṭṭhānantika), removal ending with decision (sanniṭṭhānantika), and removal ending with the cutting off of expectation (āsāvacchedika) occur both within and outside the boundary. The interim removal (antarubbhāra) depends on the Saṅgha. Removal ending with departure, completion, decision, and crossing the boundary depend on the individual. The remaining types of removal are the opposite of these two.

In that context (of the Kathina training rule), the phrase "when the robe is finished" (niṭṭhita-cīvarasmiṃ) indicates only the absence of the impediment of robes, not the absence of the impediment of residence. If it is asked: "Does the phrase 'when the Kathina is removed' (ubbhatasmiṃ kathine) not indicate the absence of both impediments? Therefore, should not that phrase alone be used to show the absence of both?" The answer is: No, because of the need for specification. How so? Indeed, because some removals of the Kathina have different cessations, and because of the dependence or non-dependence on the Saṅgha or the individual, and because of the consistency or inconsistency regarding being within or outside the boundary, the phrase 'when the Kathina is removed' is a general term (sāmañña-vacana), as the Kathina may be removed for the Saṅgha but not yet for the individual. Therefore, it is specified by the phrase 'when the robe is finished.'

What is meant is this: Even when the Kathina is removed by the Saṅgha through an interim removal, a monk who has gone outside the boundary with the impediment of robes not yet severed, who later returns to his own boundary and whose robes are not yet finished, still receives the benefits of the Kathina. To show this, it should be understood that the Buddha said 'when the robe is finished.' In this context, the 'impediment of residence' (āvာsa-palibodha) means either residing in that monastery or departing while still having concern for it. The 'impediment of robes' (cīvara-palibodha) means the robe...
66:
It consists of the robe not being made at all, being made but not finished, and the desire for the robe not yet being severed. Absence of impediment (apalibodha) should be understood as the opposite of those impediments of residence (āvāsa) and robes (cīvara). Among those co-existent states, monks who have not spread the kaṭhina always obtain the four benefits of kaṭhina during the robe-season. However, they do not always obtain the benefit of traveling without taking the determined robe (asamādānacāra). Because it is not always obtainable, the Sāsaṅka training rule was taught.

If it is asked, "How do the four benefits always accrue to monks who have not spread the kaṭhina?"—According to the statement, "When the kaṭhina is not spread, the robe-season is the last month of the rainy season," the benefit of keeping as many robes as desired (yāvadatthacīvara) during that month is evident for monks who have not spread the kaṭhina. Similarly, in the third Kaṭhina training rule (the Akālacīvara training rule), if an out-of-season robe is received from the Saṅgha starting from the time of seeking the rainy-season robe, it should be kept until the end of the robe-season, then distributed and taken. If it is a personal robe, it is allowable to keep it without determination (adhiṭṭhāna) or assignment (vikappanā) from the fifth day of the sixth fortnight of the rainy season until the end of the robe-season. This is because it is permitted by the Accekacīvara training rule. Beyond that period, it is not allowable. This is because robes arising at that time are prohibited by the first Kaṭhina training rule. It should be understood that the method mentioned in the Commentary regarding that Accekacīvara training rule refers to robes belonging to the Saṅgha, and the same is stated in the Porāṇa-gaṇṭhipada.

In the first Kaṭhina training rule, according to the first regulation or generally according to all training rules, an offense is committed on the eleventh day. This is because, to prohibit the period within the rainy season, the Commentary states, "When the robe is finished, when the kaṭhina is removed." This same method applies to the second and third training rules. Therefore, a robe obtained before or during the robe-season does not receive protection (the right to be kept) for even a single day beyond the robe-season. If it were to receive it, it would contradict the Accekacīvara training rule. For in that training rule it is taught: "It may be kept throughout the robe-season; if it is kept beyond that, there is an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya)."

An offense is incurred only by exceeding the robe-season with an urgent robe (accekacīvara) that was received from the Saṅgha as a rainy-season robe and has become one's own property after the residence. It should be understood that the offense is not incurred by exceeding the urgent-robe period (accekacīvara-kāla). According to the teaching, "Robes arising within the eleven months when the kaṭhina is not spread," the benefit that robes arising in that monastery will belong to those monks is fulfilled. Since it is taught in the Anāmantacāra and Gaṇabhojana training rules as "except at the right time," the remaining two benefits are also fulfilled. Therefore, according to the teaching, "This robe, given specifically even during the robe-season, is an out-of-season robe," a robe given specifically does not receive the ten-day protection.

Alternatively, if it is asked whether the robe still receives protection if the kaṭhina is removed during the later Kattika period because it is said "when the kaṭhina is removed"—it should not be said that it does. This is because the six instances are taught in consideration of and in comparison with other factors.
67:
These six points are taught with consideration (sāpekkhata). They are: the fourth legal issue (adhikaraṇa) in the two Duṭṭhadosa rules; the seclusion of the ear (sotassa raho) in the first Aniyata rule; the robe given specifically (ādissa dinnaṃ cīvaraṃ) in the third Kathina rule; the phrase "having made a mark, it should be laid aside" (saññāṇaṃ katvā nikkhipitabbaṃ) in the Acceka-cīvara rule; the legal issue and the word "Pārājika" in the two rules on reporting and concealing gross offenses (duṭṭhullārocana and duṭṭhullappaṭicchādana); and the phrase "by any one of the eight grounds" (aṭṭhannaṃ mātikānaṃ aññatarāya) in the three Kathina rules.

In that context (the third Kathina rule), the "robe given specifically" refers to Saṅgha-owned robes intended for distribution (saṅghika bhājitabba-cīvara); it does not refer to personal robes. The phrase "having made a mark, it should be laid aside" refers to the rainy-season robe (vassāvāsika-cīvara). A monk who has not yet completed the rains must make a mark because it is to be given back later; it does not refer to a personal Acceka robe obtained from relatives or those who have given an invitation. Therefore, it is clear that there are two types of Acceka robes: those inclined towards the Saṅgha and those inclined towards an individual.

Among these two types of Acceka robes, the one inclined towards the Saṅgha, being Saṅgha property, may be kept without formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) or assignment (vikappanā) until the Pavāraṇā day, starting from either the day of entering the rains (the 1st day after the full moon of Āsāḷha) or from the later period (piṭṭhisamaya, from the 1st day after the full moon of Kattika to the full moon of Nayon). The personal Acceka robe may also be kept similarly because it is given with the restriction, "Take it only when the rains are over." Such a personal Acceka robe remains the property of the donor as long as the recipient monk has not yet completed the rains. This is the special reason (visesa-hetu) in the Acceka-cīvara rule.

Based on the word, "If a monk, perceiving what is not an Acceka robe as not an Acceka robe, exceeds the robe-time, there is no offense," that fault (of Nissaggiya Pācittiya) belongs only to the monk who has an Acceka robe. One should not seek a special reason in the Vinaya by thinking that for some reason the statement "it is a contradiction" should be shown. If one asks, "Is it not authoritative only because it is the Buddha's domain?" No, if it were taken as authoritative in that way (without seeking a special reason), then even an Acceka robe that is one's own property in this Acceka-cīvara rule would only have to be marked and laid aside; it could not be determined, assigned, or forfeited. Then, one would have to accept a contradiction with the words, "There is no offense if, within the time, one determines, assigns, or forfeits it."

Similarly, one would have to accept a contradiction in meaning with the word, "When the removal of the Kathina is performed in the last month of the rainy season, if one exceeds the day of Kathina removal while the Kathina is spread in that month, it is a Nissaggiya." In the explanation of that Acceka-cīvara rule, it is said, "If it is not an Acceka robe, there is no offense," and that robe is indeed one that has not yet been determined or assigned; this much is the special reason. If this robe is an extra robe (atireka-cīvara), there is an offense by the first rule; if it is another robe that can be determined or assigned, there is no offense. For this meaning, this is the Blessed One's special reason. Similarly, a robe given like an Acceka robe for the sake of the Saṅgha's rainy-season residence on the full moon day of Kattika, which has not yet reached more than ten days...
68:
...should not be accepted; it should only be accepted ten days before the full moon of Kattika. This much is the special reason. Because of that meaning, a contradiction with the method of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) would also have to be accepted. In that Commentary, another method is shown by saying, "An Acceka robe that arises after being determined is not an Acceka robe." In the ancient glossary (Gaṇṭhipada), that method is not rejected either, saying it does not contradict because it was said with reference to Saṅgha property. Just as a non-Acceka robe obtained from the 6th day of the waxing moon may be accepted even on a day exceeding ten days, and there is no offense even for one who exceeds the robe-time after accepting it—this method would also have to be accepted. If so, it would contradict the first Kathina rule. If it is said that it should only be accepted ten days before, and there is no offense for one who exceeds the robe-time after accepting it, the special reason is that such a robe receives two ten-day periods of protection.

If it is argued that because it enters the robe-time—a zone of no offense—in the interval, it receives another ten days just like a robe that is determined and then withdrawn, that is not so. If it is argued that entering the season is like formal determination, that is not so. This would lead to a contradiction with the word, "Determine the rain-cloth for the four months of the rainy season, and assign it after that," because then there would be no offense even for one who does not assign it for ten days after those four months. Furthermore, it is said in the Commentary: "If the rain-cloth is obtained and finished during the rains, it must be determined within ten days; if it is finished after ten days, it must be determined on that very day; if ten days are not sufficient, one must not exceed the robe-time." Therefore, one would not be freed from the offense. This is because entering the season is not a substitute (pariyāya) for determination. By this much, the aforementioned alternative interpretation of the meaning is established by the method of the Pāḷi text itself.

Alternatively, regarding what is said in the Commentary, "If ten days are not sufficient, one must not exceed the robe-time," this meaning is completed as: even if it arises during the robe-time and ten days are not sufficient, if there is nothing to be done, one must not exceed the robe-time for that Acceka robe, just like an out-of-season robe (akāla-cīvara). According to the Pāḷi, if that robe arises within the season, even if it arises when ten days are not sufficient, such an Acceka robe is not a true Acceka robe. This is because that robe does not reach the designation of "Acceka robe" by virtue of that specific time. For has it not been taught thus: "An Acceka robe means one wishes to go with the army, or wishes to go on a journey, or is ill, or is pregnant..."?
69:
A robe offered with the words "I will give a rains-residence robe" due to the arising of faith in one who was faithless, etc., is called an acceka (emergency) robe. Therefore, just as that acceka robe should not be kept beyond the robe-time, it is established that a non-acceka robe should also not be kept beyond it. Because of this, it is stated in the Commentary: "Even if ten days are not sufficient, the robe-time should not be exceeded." Alternatively, if this is the case, the Blessed One laid down that acceka-cīvara training rule for the purpose of showing this specific meaning: "An acceka robe must not be kept beyond the robe-time."

In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, however, this training rule is stated thus: "Although this is actually established by the first kaṭhina training rule, 'An extra robe may be kept for a maximum of ten days,' the training rule was established by showing the meaning as if it were new, by way of the occasion of its arising, for the purpose of explaining a specific meaning." Therefore, it is established that it was spoken for the purpose of showing that specific meaning. Thus, it should be understood that any robe whatsoever should not be kept beyond the robe-time season. Furthermore, there is a statement in the Commentary: "A non-acceka robe arising from the sixth day onwards, or a robe that has been kept after being relinquished (paccuddhāra), also receives this protection of an acceka robe." By this statement, "If one exceeds the robe-time while perceiving a non-acceka robe as non-acceka, there is no offense," it is shown that even a non-acceka robe receives the protection of an acceka robe.

By this much, the aforementioned second alternative meaning has been established according to the method of the Pali and the method of the Commentary. Thus, the additional explanation from the mixed discourse has been expanded from the subsequent text; this is the unmixed discourse.

There are two impediments (palibodha): the impediment of robes (cīvara-palibodha) and the impediment of residence (āvāsa-palibodha). If even one of these two impediments exists, one receives the kaṭhina privileges such as "wandering without informing" (anāmantacāra), etc. To show that these impediments no longer exist in this first kaṭhina training rule, it is said: "When the robe is finished by the monk, when the kaṭhina is removed." Therefore, it is said: "For a monk who has spread the kaṭhina," and so on. In the text "kaṭhinatthārārahassa", it is said: "A person endowed with eight factors is fit to spread the kaṭhina: he knows the preliminary duties (pubbakaraṇa), he knows the relinquishing (paccuddhāra), he knows the determination (adhiṭṭhāna), he knows the spreading (atthāra), he knows the headings (mātikā), he knows the impediments (palibodha), he knows the removal (uddhāra), and he knows the privileges (ānisaṃsa)." Due to this statement, a person endowed with these eight factors is called one fit to spread the kaṭhina. Preliminary duties (pubbakaraṇa) means performing the washing, arranging, cutting, sewing, dyeing, and making the mark (kappabindu).
70:
After showing the type and size of robes by way of the Pali text "Robes means: linen," etc., now, to show the extra robe (atireka-cīvara), it is stated in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Aṭṭhakathā: "But what was said regarding those determined and assigned," and so on. Although it is said "noting the place where it is kept," in whatever place a robe is kept, whether that robe is behind the person (who makes the determination) or not, the determination (adhiṭṭhāna) is indeed effective. Whether it was kept there before or after is not the essential measure.

For a monk who has committed an ultimate offense (antimavatthu), the act of wearing white clothes or abandoning the dyed robes that were habitually worn, by way of renouncing the state of a monk, is called "returning to the lower life" (hīnāyāvattana).

"At the dawn-rise of the eleventh day" means, excluding the final dawn (the 1st day of the waning moon of Kattika), it should be understood as the dawn prior to that (the 10th day). There, "final" means the first dawn-rise of the 1st day of the waning moon of the later Kattika. Since that dawn is within the (allowed) time, it does not cause a nissaggiya (forfeiture) offense. In this (first kaṭhina training rule), the instrumental case in "by the monk when the robe is finished" (niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunā) is an instrumental case that does not regard the origin (nidāna), because there is no agent in the origin. Therefore, it is said that "a maximum of ten days" is the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) in this context. Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow the triple robe to be determined, not to be assigned," etc., the general statement in this training rule "he assigns" (vikappeti) without specification seems contradictory. However, the Tathāgatas do not speak contradictory words. Therefore, the meaning should be understood thus: I allow the triple robe to be determined only for the purpose of carrying it as a triple robe, not to be assigned. But for the rain-cloth (vassikasāṭika), I allow it only to be assigned after the four months (of the rains), not to be determined. This being so, if a monk wishes to be away from one of the robes among the triple robe, he is given the opportunity to assign it for the sake of the comfort of being away after relinquishing the determination of the triple robe, and there is no offense even if ten days are exceeded. By this method, it is written that it should be understood that assignment is not prohibited for any robe.

The summary decision of this training rule is: "When the robe is finished," etc., is said with reference to a robe that arises starting from the first day of the winter (the 1st day of the waning moon of Kattika) when the kaṭhina has not been spread, or starting from the first day of the summer (the 1st day of the waning moon of Phagguna) when the kaṭhina has been spread. Here, the objector says: "Because of the commentary statement 'The determination of one who has the robes washed and made white by laundrymen is also a firm determination,' the determination is effective even on an undyed robe." If so, should a regulation be made that one must determine only after sewing, dyeing, and making the mark (kappabindu), or should it not be made? It should indeed be made. Just as an alms-bowl that has been determined does not lose its determination even if it later becomes white or red, however...
71:
Just as such an alms-bowl does not come under determination (adhiṭṭhāna), this robe should be understood in the same way. If one thinks, "Tomorrow I will remove the Kaṭhina," and does not determine the robe received today (the day before removal), a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense is incurred as soon as dawn rises. Why? Because the training rule was taught starting with "Niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ" (Pārājika, 462-463). During the Kaṭhina period, protection can be obtained for more than ten days, but after the Kaṭhina is removed, it cannot be obtained even for a single day.

For example, the Saṅgha that has spread the Kaṭhina receives the benefits regarding the three robes from the day of spreading until the removal; not after that. Similarly, a monk receives protection from the day of spreading until removal, but once the Kaṭhina is removed, he does not receive it even for a single day. Here, one might ask: "Can one still get ten days starting from the day of removal?" The answer is: "No." Why? Because the Blessed One said: "Monks, I allow an extra robe to be kept for at most ten days."

Even within the Kaṭhina period, a Nissaggiya offense might seem to occur at dawn on the eleventh day. However, to prevent such an excess, "Niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ" etc. was taught. It was not taught to show that Kaṭhina days are not days. This meaning will become clear in various texts.

Alternatively, the rainy season robe (vassikasāṭika) of standard size should be determined for the four months of the rainy season as mentioned. After those four months, it should be relinquished and shared (vikappanā). In this context, the phrase "having relinquished" means it must be relinquished and shared on the Uposatha day of the full moon of Kattika. This is because after that day, starting from the first day of the cold season (the first waning day of Kattika), there is no more determination. In this way, a robe arising during the Kaṭhina period should also be known to be determined about a day before the Kaṭhina is removed.

## The Commentary on the Kaṭhina Training Rule is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Udosito Training Rule
"For a monk who has spread the Kaṭhina, there is no offense if he leaves his robe anywhere within a bound boundary (baddha-sīmā) and departs for five months," is stated in the Commentary. The statement "It is also allowable in an unbound boundary (abaddha-sīmā)" establishes the spreading of Kaṭhina in an unbound boundary and the forest-dweller's training rule (āraññaka-sikkhāpada). Now—

This miscellaneous (pakiṇṇaka) decision should be understood: regarding the cut robe, the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) of the three robes, the training rule concerning suspected areas (sāsaṅka-sammata), the upper robe along with the inner robe, and the non-offense for a monk without a robe due to the completion of relinquishment etc.
72:
In this miscellaneous discussion, the following is a decision preceded by an objection. Some teachers, because of the words "a double-layered outer robe" (Mahāvagga), say: "A single-layered outer robe should not be determined; if it is determined, the determination does not take effect." Therefore, they give only a double-layered outer robe to candidates for ordination and ordain them. These teachers should be informed by this hint from the Sutta (suttalesa). The Blessed One first allowed "a cut outer robe, a cut upper robe, and a cut inner robe." Then, in the case where "when the three robes were being made for a certain monk, there was not enough to cut all of them; or not enough if two were cut and one was not; or not enough if one was cut and two were not," He allowed: "Monks, I allow an extra layer (anvādhika) to be added." Therefore, it is established that even a single-layered outer robe is allowable. If a robe is not enough even when cut, how could it be double-layered? In the Commentary also, it is said: "To add an extra layer means to give an additional piece of cloth; this additional piece should be added only to a robe that is insufficient. If it is sufficient, an additional piece is not allowable; it must simply be cut." In the case of a Kaṭhina robe, however, because it has its own unique characteristics and because there is no statement saying "a cut robe is insufficient for a double layer," the conclusion should be reached here that only a cut robe is allowable.

Regarding the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga): Since novices (sāmaṇeras) do not have the dhutaṅga of the three robes, should it not be said that one is a "three-robe-wearer" only with three robes, and since they do not have determination, "only with a determined robe"? No, it should not be said so. Because it would contradict the breaking of the dhutaṅga. The dhutaṅga is broken only by consenting to a fourth robe, not by being away from the three robes, nor by consenting to an extra robe, nor by wearing an extra robe. However, since the Blessed One allowed nine types of robes for monks by way of determination and spoke of them by way of their nature, but did not do so for novices because they have no regulation of robes like householders, that dhutaṅga was not allowed for them. Therefore, since there is no mention of the procedure for undertaking it for novices, this conclusion should be reached.

Regarding "Sāsaṅka-sammata" (considered suspicious): In the Sāsaṅka training rule of the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary, the factors for an offense are not stated separately. It only says, "The rest should be understood in the same way as stated in the second training rule of the Robe Chapter (Cīvara-vagga)." However, that factor is not directly stated there. In that (Udosito) training rule, being away from the robe for a night is the fourth factor; in this (Sāsaṅka) training rule, being away for six nights is the factor. This is the distinction here. Therefore, because of the similarity of factors and the similarity of formal agreement (sammuti), this training rule is known as the Sāsaṅka training rule.
73:
This (Udosita) training rule is without exception (nippadesa), while that (Sāsaṅka) training rule has exceptions (sappadesa) [in its application]. This is because the Sāsaṅka training rule is limited only to the month of Kattika (the period allowed for keeping robes). In that Sāsaṅka training rule, even if a monk is outside the village, if he enters the village boundary (gāmasīmā), stays there until the dawn of the seventh day, and then departs, he incurs no offense. In this (Udosita) training rule, however, it is not so. In this training rule, a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense is incurred at every successive dawn (day by day). In that Sāsaṅka training rule, the offense is incurred only at the dawn of the seventh day. This is the distinction between these two training rules.

As for the factors regarding the inability to keep the robes, they are not mentioned here because they are established by the reverse of the factors for the completeness of robe-keeping, and by the method already stated in this training rule. Although those factors are not mentioned, the fourth factor should have been distinguished; however, it was not. For what reason? It is because, in this training rule, one must confess the offense after forfeiting the robe according to the stated order of forfeiture, and it is intended to clarify the release from the offense incurred in that Sāsaṅka training rule. Even if one is separated from the robe for a whole year, it is considered as being separated for only one night; how much more so for a separation of six nights? Even so, if the factors mentioned in that Sāsaṅka training rule are present, one must forfeit the robe according to the method stated there. If one forfeits it in the winter or summer, the fourth factor was not distinguished in order to make it known that it is also proper to forfeit according to the method stated in this training rule—so say the teachers.

A robe that has exceeded one month, and also exceeded ten days, is indeed forfeited by saying, "It has exceeded ten days." Some teachers say that even if it has not reached a month, it is forfeited by saying, "It has exceeded ten days" or "It has exceeded a month." Nevertheless, if it is a robe for which there is still hope of receiving (paccāsācīvara), it becomes a Nissaggiya. In that case, it should be forfeited by saying, "It has exceeded ten days," but for the original robe, it should be forfeited by saying, "It has exceeded a month."

When it is said "santaruṭṭhara" or "saṅghāṭi" or "cīvara," does it refer only to the triple robe (ticīvara) or to other robes as well? In this matter—if only the triple robe were prohibited, it would contradict the training rules such as acchinnacīvara (stolen robe), acchandana (not being covered), dhovāpana (having a robe washed), and viññatti (requesting a robe). If it refers to other robes as well, it would contradict phrases such as "niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ" (when the robe is finished). The answer is: it should not be taken as a fixed rule; it should be understood according to the circumstances. Thus, in passages such as "having left the robes, he wanders through the countryside with only the santaruṭṭhara," it refers only to the triple robe. In passages such as "Monks, one should not enter a village with only the santaruṭṭhara; one should accept a robe at most as a santaruṭṭhara," it refers to any robe. Similarly, in passages such as "the saṅghāṭis should be given in layers, the inner robe (nivāsana) should be given, the saṅghāṭi should be given; here, friend, is a saṅghāṭi for you, give me a cloth," it is the same. For it is said, "Every robe is called 'saṅghāṭi' in the sense of being joined together." Some say that in the phrase "niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ," it is also the same. Some say that since robes are allowed as much as needed during the robe-season, if all of them were being made, they would never be finished; therefore, it refers only to the triple robe.
74:
What is meant by the statement, "There is no offense for one without a robe because of the success of paccuddhara (relinquishing determination), etc."? Some teachers say that for the sake of not making the Udosita training rule purposeless, when one is separated from the triple robe, an offense is incurred for all three robes. To that, this is the reply: there is no offense because of the success of paccuddhara, etc. For it is said (in the Pārājika Pali), "There is no offense if one relinquishes (paccuddharati) or gives away (vissajjeti) the robe before dawn." Otherwise, for one who relinquishes or gives away before dawn, as long as another person does not determine (adhiṭṭhāti) it, he would incur an offense according to the method already stated. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "separation by seven abbhantaras," it should be understood that if there is separation as literally stated, an offense is incurred due to separation within seven abbhantaras; if there is no separation, there is no offense.

## The Explanation of the Udosita Training Rule is Finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Akālacīvara Training Rule

Because it is difficult to recognize the place suitable for a fence in a monastery that is not fenced, "api ca bhikkhūnaṃ," etc., was said (in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary) to show that place. It should be understood as: from the place where monks regularly assemble at the edge of the monastery, or from the dining hall situated at the edge, or from the dwelling where monks constantly reside. If monks sitting together in a monastery form a continuous line extending for a hundred yojanas, the access boundary (upacārasīmā) extends for a hundred yojanas. When it is said, "I give to the samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā (boundary of common communion)," it does not reach those staying in the khaṇḍasīmā (small boundary), etc., because those are separate samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmās. This is the difference between the samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā and the avippavāsa-sīmā (boundary of non-separation). A gift given with the words "I give to the avippavāsa-sīmā" does not reach those staying in the village. Why? Because of the statement (in the Mahāvagga Pali), "excluding the village and the village precinct (gāmūpacāra)." However, a gift given with the words "I give to the samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā" reaches those staying where there is an avippavāsa-sīmā, as well as those staying elsewhere. It is also said, "It reaches those staying there," and "When one stands in a khaṇḍasīmā and says, 'Let the Saṅgha within the boundary receive it,' it should be distributed by defining it only by the upacārasīmā." Furthermore, it is said, "It reaches them even if they are outside the boundary as long as the Kathina has not been dismantled," and "When the Kathina has not been spread, if one enters the monastery during the four months of winter and says, 'I give to the Saṅgha that has completed the Vassa,' it reaches even those who are outside the boundary, provided they completed the latter Vassa without breaking it." Thus the Vinaya experts (Vinayadharas) decide, though it is not directly mentioned in the Commentary. Therefore, it is said in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary, "Those who know the characteristics say..." and "Starting from the robe-month..."
75:
If it is said, 'We offer the rains-residence robe (vassāvāsika) until the full moon day of Phagguna (Tabaung), the last day of the cold season,' there is a statement in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary that it reaches only those monks who have resided for the entire past rains-residence, whether the Kathina has been spread or not. In this regard, the decision is written that if the Kathina has been spread, the monks who completed the first rains-residence receive it for five months; if the Kathina has not been spread, they receive it for four months.

'Those by whom my rice gruel (yāgu) was drunk' means those invited monks by whom my rice gruel was drunk. Therefore, the Commentary states that it reaches only those monks who were invited and drank the rice gruel. Alternatively, if interpreted differently, when it is said 'those by whom my rice gruel was drunk,' it is said that it should reach all those monks who drank the rice gruel, whether they were invited or not. In this Akālacīvara training rule, the Buddha, by saying 'when the robe is finished, when the Kathina is removed,' makes it known that the three types of out-of-season robes (akālacīvara) do not arise during this Kathina period. Even so, why are the three types of out-of-season robes explained in detail in the Padabhājanī?

To answer: This training rule is not stated with reference to the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna). Rather, in the first Kathina training rule, only ten days were permitted; however, if the robe is insufficient within those ten days and there is hope of obtaining more, the Buddha intended to extend those ten days to one month. This specific meaning is shown here. Although an out-of-season robe should be distributed by the monks present, this training rule extends the permission by saying 'it should be accepted by a monk who desires it.' Therefore, all three types of out-of-season robes are explained in detail in the Padabhājanī.

'It should be made quickly' means it should be made quickly within ten days. This explanatory statement was made by the Commentator to indicate the characteristic of the previous training rule when the robe material is sufficient. Therefore, it should be understood that 'ten days' is mentioned instead of just saying 'quickly' or 'speedily.' While this is the case for a monk whose Kathina is spread, if a question arises regarding a monk whose Kathina is not spread, it is shown that it is prohibited for him. At that time, the objector, having received the answer and seeing no further grounds for objection, reaches a state of frustration; so writes the teacher Vajirabuddhi.

## The Explanation of the Akālacīvara Training Rule is finished.

## 4. The Explanation of the Purāṇacīvara Training Rule

If it is asked whether the statement in this training rule, 'even in the pure Bhikkhu Sangha like the Sakyan princesses,' contradicts the Pāḷi text which says 'A Bhikkhunī is one ordained by both Sanghas,' it does not contradict...
76:
...because the intention (meaning) is understood. Since ordination in the presence of monks alone is prohibited for nuns, this was stated to avoid the implication that a Bhikkhunī is only one ordained by both Sanghas.

'By one matter' means due to any one of the first commands such as washing, dyeing, or beating (a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense is incurred). 'Washes without being told' means a nun who was not commanded performs the washing, dyeing, or beating. The teacher Vajirabuddhi wrote that because it is said 'without being told,' there is no offense if a nun performs washing etc. without being commanded. In this Purāṇacīvara training rule, 'robe' refers only to the inner robe and the upper robe that are fit to be worn. If it is argued that 'it should only be called a robe fit to be worn,' it is not necessary to say so because the term 'old robe' (purāṇacīvara) already establishes that it is a robe fit to be worn. This was also taught in the Padabhājanī: 'An old robe is one that has been worn even once or used as a wrap even once.'

## The Explanation of the Purāṇacīvara Training Rule is finished.

## 5. The Explanation of the Cīvarappaṭiggahaṇa Training Rule

## 7. The Explanation of the Tatuttari Training Rule

By nature, one wanders with only the inner and upper robes, either due to the Kathina-palibodha (impediment) or due to the Sāsaṅka training rule. In this regard, hearing the words of people who were complaining, 'They will request many robes without knowing the limit, or they will trade in cloth,' etc., the Buddha [addressed] the group of six monks...
77:
“Monks, O empty men, why do you ask for many robes without knowing the limit?” (Pārā. 522). Because the training rule was prescribed after this was said, and because it is stated in this Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, “It is prescribed in the case of asking for many robes,” and because it is stated in the Samantapāsādikā, “Monks whose robes have not been snatched away are not allowed to break off branches and leaves for themselves, but they are allowed to do so for monks whose robes have been snatched away,” if it is asked whether it is allowable to ask for a robe of a certain measure for another monk, the answer is: it is not allowable. Why? Because in the very origin (aṭṭhuppatti) of the Aññātakaviññatti Sikkhāpada, asking from non-relatives is prohibited. In the Anāpatti Pāḷi of that rule (Pārā. 521), it is prohibited by the words “for another,” meaning when asking for another monk, one must ask only from that monk's relatives or those who have given an invitation, and not from others. Therefore, the Blessed One also, having rebuked them, saying, “You ask for many robes,” and when prescribing the rule, allowed the acceptance according to the measure only in the manner stated as “I will bring [robes] and invite [you],” but He did not allow asking for a robe of a certain measure for another monk. Since this rule was prescribed in the very case of asking for another monk, the phrase “for another” was not mentioned here; it was not because it is not obtainable.

In the ancient Commentaries, it is said: “In the case of relatives and those who have given an invitation, even many [robes] are normally allowable; but due to the reason of robes being snatched away, only the [specified] measure is allowable.” Since it is stated in the Samantapāsādikā (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.526) that this statement does not agree with the Anāpatti Pāḷi which says, “There is no offense in the case of relatives and those who have given an invitation” (Pārā. 526), it is written here also according to the aforementioned method that there is no offense for a monk who asks from relatives or those who have given an invitation, or for a monk who purchases with his own property. Although the phrase “for another” was not spoken because it contradicts the preamble (nidāna), the teachers say that it is indeed obtainable according to the aforementioned method.

## 9. Explanation of the Second Upakkhaṭa Sikkhāpada

If it is asked, “What is the purpose of the second Upakkhaṭa Sikkhāpada?” the answer would be that there is no purpose. However, it was prescribed solely by the power of the circumstances of the rule's origin (aṭṭhuppatti), like the Bhikkhunī's rule on sitting in private (raho-nisajja). If this were the case, the Elders who conducted the Council (Saṅgītikārakas) should not have included it in the Council, because the meaning is achieved even without it, it does not override [the first rule], and permission was given not to include [minor rules]. For it was said: “Ānanda, if the Saṅgha wishes... it may abolish [the minor and lesser rules]” (Dī. Ni. 2.216, Cūḷava. 441).

All this is not the reason. For the Buddhas do not utter words that are purposeless, much less a training rule. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: “The meaning should be understood in this very way. For this is similar to a supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) of the previous one,” and so on. A supplementary regulation is also not without purpose. Since this rule is similar to that, it is shown that it is not without purpose.

If so, what special meaning is there in this rule? To answer that, it is said: “In that [first] rule, only one person is distressed; here, two are distressed. This is the distinction here.” By this special meaning, what other additional meaning is shown? In the ancient Gaṇṭhipada, it is said: “The additional meaning shown is that even in a single case, it is not proper to cause distress to two persons.” Therefore, this shows: “The count of offenses is not only by the count of robes received, but also by the count of objects, namely the persons distressed.”

There are these verses here:
“This second Upakkhaṭa [rule] is taught here for the purpose of showing that there may be many offenses even by the count of objects (persons).
It is like in the analysis (vibhaṅga) of the Kāyasaṃsagga rule, where there are many offenses even with one woman due to the [number of] actions (payoga).” (Vajira. Ṭī. Pārājika 532).

Furthermore, it should be understood that this rule has the purpose of showing the decision to be taken in all rules of a similar nature. It is said:
“For the purpose of showing the occurrence of such procedures as the multiplicity and mixture of offenses,
due to the multiplicity and mixture of unrelated bhikkhunīs,
the Teacher spoke this second Upakkhaṭa rule.” (Vajira. Ṭī. Pārājika 532).
79:
The investigation preceded by the summary meaning of that verse is as follows: If a monk causes a single old robe to be washed by two or many bhikkhunīs, the number of Pācittiya offenses corresponds to the number of bhikkhunīs. Similarly, if he receives a single robe shared by two or many [bhikkhunīs], other than by exchange, the number of offenses is the same. In this Second Ukkhaṭa Sikkhāpada as well, if he requests a single robe shared by two or many, the number of offenses corresponds to the number of persons requested. Likewise, in other training rules of this nature, this method should be applied. This is first the method regarding multiplicity (bahutā).

Regarding mixing (vimissatā): If he causes a single robe to be washed by a bhikkhunī who is a relative and one who is a non-relative, and if [the work] is completed at the same time, one Pācittiya offense is incurred. If the relative bhikkhunī washes a little first and then the non-relative bhikkhunī washes it well to completion, a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense is incurred. If the non-relative bhikkhunī washes first and then the relative bhikkhunī washes it well to completion, only a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred by the monk due to the effort of the non-relative bhikkhunī. If he causes it to be washed while perceiving both the non-relative and the relative bhikkhunī as non-relatives, or having doubt, or perceiving them as relatives, the number of various offenses such as Nissaggiya and Dukkaṭa should be understood according to the method already stated. Similarly, if he receives a robe owned by both a non-relative and a relative bhikkhunī, given by both together, only a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense is incurred. If he receives it from the hand of the non-relative bhikkhunī only, only a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense is incurred. If he receives it from the hand of the relative bhikkhunī, there is no offense. If he has perceptions such as 'non-relative' regarding both of them, the number of various offenses such as Nissaggiya and Dukkaṭa should be understood according to the method already stated. Similarly, in cases such as requesting from a non-relative, the method should be applied as applicable. This is the method regarding mixing (vimissatā).

By the word 'ādi' (etc.), if he requests from many non-relatives, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred according to the number of persons requested. If one gives and another does not, a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense is incurred. If one whom he did not request from gives, there is no Nissaggiya offense. If the one who was requested gives a robe owned by both the one requested and the one not requested, a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense is incurred. If both give, only a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense is incurred. If the one not requested gives, he is free from the Nissaggiya offense. If the one not requested gives at the word of the one requested, there is no offense. Similarly, in the Ukkhaṭa Sikkhāpada and others, the method should be applied as applicable.

By this much, the meaning of the verse beginning with 'Aññātikāya' has been stated in brief. In the explanation of this Second Ukkhaṭa Sikkhāpada, regarding the Rahonisajja Sikkhāpada of a bhikkhunī as being without purpose...

## 10. Rāja Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

Some teachers say that because it is said, 'It destroys the standing, it ruins the reason for coming,' he does not get to request again. Some say that because hospitality (paṭisanthāra) was performed, the monk's coming is without purpose and he will not receive the robe. Some say this is stated because it does not have the characteristic of requesting. However, the Elder Upatissa says, 'Hospitality should not be performed because of the intention to preach the Dhamma, etc. "Ruining the reason for coming" means destroying the standing for the sake of requesting; because he did what should not be done while wishing to request, the duty is broken and a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred.'

The Elder Dhammasiri says, 'If he sits on a seat, by sitting once, he destroys the standing twice. If he receives material gifts (āmisa), by receiving once, he destroys the standing twice. If he preaches the Dhamma, by a single word within the limit stated in the Dhamma-desanā Sikkhāpada, he destroys the standing twice. It is with reference to such destruction of the standing that it is said, "it ruins the reason for coming."' 

There are four persons pointed out by the monk: the first one made known by saying, 'This person...'; the second one of whom it is said, 'This person is an attendant (veyyāvaccakara)... even if not told, it is proper to request'; the third one of whom it is said, even while the messenger is going, 'I will give into his hand,' etc.; and the fourth one of whom it is said, 'He sends another to inform.' Just as there are four pointed out by the monk, there are also four pointed out by the messenger. The teacher Vajirabuddhi wrote that in the case of a kappiya-kāraka who speaks openly (mukhavēvaṭika) and a kappiya-kāraka who is not present (parammukha), one should act as towards those who are non-relatives and have not given invitation (appavārita).

Because of the word "having weighed" (tulayitvā), when weighing with a scale, the black wool should not exceed the limit, and at most, two parts of black wool should be taken. ## 4. Commentary on the Chabbassa Sikkhāpada

Because it is taught "within six years," it is only allowable to make a new rug when six years are complete. Therefore, the six-year period should be understood as starting from the day the rug is finished. In making this new rug, all rugs made either after six years have passed or by the power of the formal agreement (sammuti) given to a sick monk are allowable to be used together. Since a single rug is not sufficient for a sick monk, many new rugs are also allowable. Some teachers say that from the time the illness subsides and the monk is able to carry the rug and go, neither the formal agreement nor the illness protects him (from an offense). In fact, because this training rule, which is as stainless as the Buddha for six years, is very profound to examine, it should be understood that the act should be performed only when six years are complete.

## The Commentary on the Chabbassa Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Nisīdana Sikkhāpada

In this Nisīdana Sikkhāpada, why did the Buddha not prescribe the training rule as "a monk [making] a rug..." but instead prescribed it by adding the word nisīdana as "a sitting rug..."? Must there not be a reason for prescribing it in this way? There is a reason. Because monks were discarding rugs with the perception that they were a fourth robe, the Blessed One prescribed it thus for the purpose of showing those monks that those rugs are not robes. Therefore, those monks, fearing the breaking of the triple-robe ascetic practice (tecīvarika dhutaṅga), discarded the rugs with the perception of them being a fourth robe and undertook the thirteen ascetic practices. The Blessed One also allowed the rug for those monks. After that, it occurred to those monks: "The Blessed One did not allow this sitting rug, which has the form of a sitting-cloth robe, as a fourth robe; how much less would He allow a rug that has already been made?" Therefore, the meaning is that the Blessed One prescribed it as a "sitting rug" instead of just a "rug" for the purpose of preventing the perception of a robe from arising in those monks regarding the rug. Among these five types of rugs, the first three are not allowable to use even if regained after performing a disciplinary act (vinayakamma) because they are unallowable (akappiya). The last two are allowable; so it is written by the teacher Vajirabuddhi. If one asks how this is known, it should be understood that it is known from the teaching: "There is no offense if one regains and uses a rug made by another."

## The Commentary on the Nisīdana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 6. Eḷakalomavikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

By the words “addānamaggappaṭipannassa” (for one who has set out on a long journey), it is shown that for a monk who is naturally traveling on a long journey, even if sheep’s wool arises for him, it should be carried for a maximum of only three yojanas; how much more so for a monk who has not set out on a journey? If it is for a monk who has set out, this meaning is shown for a monk who travels a long distance involuntarily, just like the involuntary travel of a bhikkhunī who has completed the rains retreat. Alternatively, the connection may be made as: “For a monk traveling on a long journey, there is a nissaggiya pācittiya.” Because of that very connection, it is established that there is no offense for a monk who is designated as “one not traveling” because his effort to travel has ceased due to a desire to stay.

In this alternative interpretation, the construction should be understood as: “If sheep’s wool should arise for a monk... even if there is no carrier, for a monk traveling on a long journey, there is a nissaggiya pācittiya.” On the other hand, because the limit of three yojanas is intended from the place where the sheep’s wool originated, and for a monk who is not traveling, there is no such three-yojana limit, it is said: “If it should arise for a monk traveling on a long journey.” Therefore, it is established that there is no offense for a monk who, having recovered wool that was snatched away by thieves and so on, carries it. This is because the recovery of that wool is indeed called its “arising.”

By the words “ākaṅkhamānena bhikkhunā paṭiggahetabbāni” (they should be accepted by a monk who so desires), it is shown that an offense is incurred only for carrying wool accepted by oneself beyond three yojanas. By showing this, it is established that there is no offense for a monk who carries the property of others accepted without desire.

Although the factor of “being one’s own property” is not included among the factors of the offense, it should be understood that this meaning is shown by the phrase “if they should arise for a monk” and by the phrase “having recovered what was snatched away.” In the ancient Gaṇṭhipada, it is also said: “If he goes making another monk carry it, there is no offense for either.” Therefore, it is established that if two monks, having reached the three-yojana limit, exchange each other’s goods and carry them, there is no offense.

“They should be carried by one’s own hand for a distance of three yojanas” means they should be carried by oneself only up to three yojanas. For what purpose is it only three yojanas? It is because the boundary of a sīmā is at most this much. For it was said: “Monks, I allow you to authorize a sīmā of at most three yojanas.” (Mahāvagga 140). This three-yojana limit is also the maximum for a monk traveling with the intention to stay or with the intention to return. For it was said: “The group-of-six monks authorized very large sīmās... when monks come for the Uposatha, they arrive while the Pātimokkha is being recited, they arrive just after it has been recited, and they stay in between.” (Mahāvagga 140).

## Miscellaneous Remarks on these Training Rules

The eighth training rule prohibits taking, having someone take, or consenting to gold or silver given by another for oneself, or given as an exchange, or found as refuse-rag (paṃsukūla). The ninth training rule prohibits the exchange of gold or silver for another or for oneself.
85:
The tenth training rule is the exchange of non-monetary items (arūpiya-parivattana). The statement, "There is no offense for a monk who, perceiving a non-monetary object as a non-monetary object, engages in buying and selling with the five classes of fellow practitioners," indicates that an offense is incurred if one engages in buying and selling with anyone other than those five classes of fellow practitioners. A non-monetary object is also an object of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa-vatthu). Therefore, it is stated with certainty that if such a non-monetary object is exchanged [for a nissaggiya object], it constitutes a nissaggiya pācittiya offense. Should it be argued by the ancient teachers that "because it is connected to the non-offense clause regarding the exchange of dukkaṭa objects with the five classes of fellow practitioners, there is indeed no offense"? No, because only allowable objects (kappiya-vatthu) are mentioned in that training rule. Should it be questioned, "If a nissaggiya pācittiya offense is incurred for an allowable object, what need is there to mention an object of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa-vatthu)?" No, because the gravity or lightness of an object is not determined by the gravity or lightness of the resulting offense.

To explain in detail: although pearls, rubies, cat's-eyes, etc., are of great value, they are only objects of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa-vatthu) compared to nissaggiya objects which require forfeiture; thus, pearls and such are considered light objects (lahuka-vatthu) relative to nissaggiya objects. The commentators state that just as receiving a dukkaṭa object results in a dukkaṭa offense even if it is a light object, it is also appropriate that a dukkaṭa offense is incurred for causing the exchange of that dukkaṭa object or for exchanging with that dukkaṭa object.

Alternatively, regarding the statement "because only allowable objects are mentioned in that training rule," even if dukkaṭa objects were intended, they were not preached in the Pāḷi text for fear of complications in the non-offense section (anāpatti-vāra). If pearls and such were preached, then in the non-offense section, saying to a lay attendant (kappiya-kāraka), "We have these pearls, etc., and we have need of such-and-such cat's-eyes, etc.," would imply an offense under the tenth training rule. Because such exchanges, like informing a lay attendant, exist, it should be understood that those unallowable dukkaṭa objects were preached under the ninth training rule regarding trading with money (rūpiya-saṃvohāra). Although it is true that only allowable objects are permitted in the training rule on buying and selling (kayavikkaye), and one could say that dukkaṭa objects are also intended in the tenth training rule by this logic, it should be taken as not intended because it contradicts the Commentary.

What is the underlying reason here? Should it be questioned, "Since it is connected to the non-offense of buying and selling with the five classes of fellow practitioners, is there also no offense regarding dukkaṭa objects?" No, because dukkaṭa objects are not included in that training rule. Should it be questioned, "The reason for the exclusion of dukkaṭa objects has already been stated"? It is not because there is no special reason for obtaining a turn in the non-offense section (anāpatti-vāra) showing how there is no offense in an object that would otherwise cause an offense with the five classes of fellow practitioners. Since dukkaṭa objects are unallowable, the view of the Commentary is established that an offense must be incurred even if it is with the five classes of fellow practitioners.

Another method: If a nissaggiya pācittiya offense were to occur in buying and selling with dukkaṭa objects, the method stated for allowable objects should be applicable there, but it is not. Therefore, those dukkaṭa objects should only be mentioned in the ninth training rule. Thus, what is called "trading" (saṃvohāra) is also buying and selling (kayavikkaye) which occurs by taking the exchange of other objects in its entirety...
86: Buying and selling also occurs by taking the exchange in its entirety. Therefore, if one exchanges by saying, "Give this object for that object," setting aside buying and selling, it is not said to be "allowable." According to the method stated in the section on non-offense (anāpattivāra) of the tenth (Kāyavikkaya) training rule, because it contradicts the permission regarding forfeiture (nissaggiya) in the exchange of those (wrong-doing) objects, it is only an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in causing an exchange with a wrong-doing object, as stated in the Commentary. If it is asked, "Is there no offense of forfeiture for those objects through buying and selling?" [the answer is] no, because all exchange is called buying and selling. For this reason, it is stated [in the Samantapāsādikā]: "The statement in the Andhaka Commentary that 'if one engages in buying and selling, it is an offense of forfeiture and expiation (nissaggiya pācittiya)' is poorly stated. Why? Because there is no such thing as buying and selling other than giving and receiving." Whether this reasoning of mine is established or not, according to the method stated in the section on non-offense of the tenth training rule, which is regarded as the characteristic of buying and selling by one's own opinion, it is because it contradicts the permission regarding forfeiture in the exchange of those objects. Or, let it be; in the tenth rule, one must certainly know the allowable objects. Therefore, those objects are indeed [involved in] buying and selling and thus fall into the state of forfeiture. In this way, the view of the Commentary is established.## Here, the ancient teachers say: If one exceeds [the rule] by causing one's own gold or silver to reach the hands of another, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If one causes another's gold or silver to reach one's own hands, it is an offense of forfeiture according to the eighth (Rūpiya) training rule. What happens in the exchange of an object already received? It is considered insignificant (avvohārika). Alternatively, if one first causes another's gold or silver to reach one's own hands, it is an offense of forfeiture according to the eighth training rule because of the acceptance of gold and silver. If one later causes one's own gold or silver to reach the hands of another, it is an offense of forfeiture according to the (ninth) trading (Saṃvohāra) training rule. The statement made there (by the ancient teachers) that "by the mere act of receiving gold and silver, there is an offense according to the eighth rule, and by later exchanging, there is an offense according to the ninth rule" is appropriate. The statement "if one exceeds, it is an offense of wrong-doing" is poorly stated. The inconsistency of the offense of wrong-doing has already been shown in the procedures for forfeiture. What is meant is this: If there were to be two types of forfeiture offenses, one would have to say in the procedure for forfeiture, "Venerable Sir, I accepted gold and silver, and I also engaged in various kinds of gold and silver exchange." This is because in all the Pali texts, where it says "he causes gold and silver to be exchanged," the acceptance of gold and silver is mentioned.## By this much, what is stated in the ancient Ganthipada—"A monk who engages in buying and selling with a wrong-doing object, if he takes any one of the four forfeiture objects, there is an offense of forfeiture according to the eighth training rule. If he takes a wrong-doing object for a wrong-doing object, saying 'Give this object for that object,' there is an offense of forfeiture for that reason. If he takes it by setting aside buying and selling, it is an offense of wrong-doing. In receiving gold and silver that has been caused to be exchanged, it is forfeiture by the eighth rule; in the act of exchanging, it is forfeiture by the ninth rule," and so on—without accepting it himself, having brought it out by way of what is allowable, it is allowable to exchange with the five classes of co-religionists...
