## 1. Patta-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

Among those bowls, two are not [proper] bowls; therefore, those two bowls should be used as utensils, and it is meant that they do not come under determination (adhiṭṭhāna) or assignment (vikappanā). In 'fired in a manner suitable for a recluse,' an iron bowl is fired five times, and a clay bowl is fired twice. It is also written: 'Because the accumulation of bowls by a nun is prohibited, considering such accumulation as unsuitable for a monk as well, it is said "having relinquished the old bowl".' This statement is inappropriate because it is taught in the Pāḷi: 'To make an accumulation means a bowl that is not determined and not assigned.'

Indeed, regarding this accumulation of bowls, just like the accumulation of stores (nicaya-sannidhi) in the Kathina-khandhaka, even a single bowl is called 'accumulation' (sanniccaya) on the next day. In the subsequent training rule, however, the determination is fixed as 'the second is prohibited.' Therefore, one does not get to determine two bowls. If one determines them together, both become undetermined. If one determines them separately, the second one is undetermined. However, for assignment (vikappanā), one can have many bowls.

In the phrase 'kākaṇikamattampi,' the word 'pi' includes the firing, meaning 'it does not even produce a single firing.' Alternatively, if it is suitable with just one firing, it is allowable. Therefore, it should be understood that the number of firings was not mentioned in the Commentary. Because it is not a bowl...
88:
(That bowl) is not fit for determination (adhiṭṭhāna). "Apaccuddharantena vikappetabboti" means that a monk who does not wish to relinquish the old bowl should perform the assignment (vikappanā) of the new bowl.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Bowls (Pattasikkhāpada) is finished.

## 2. Ūnapañcabandhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

Regarding the word "pavārite" (invited), it is written that in a place invited by the Saṅgha, it is allowable only if there are five mends (pañcabandhana); however, in a place invited individually, it is allowable even with fewer than five mends.

Whatever monk, for the sake of a bowl with fewer than five mends,
Performs this practice that has been taught,
That monk, for the sake of a bowl with fewer than five mends,
Having approached (the elders), (should forfeit it).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Fewer than Five Mends (Ūnapañcabandhanasikkhāpada) is finished.

## 3. Bhesajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

By the statement "having accepted medicinal items for consumption," it is explained that it is allowable to accept and keep them for purposes such as anointing the feet. Regarding the statement "the meat of which creatures is allowable," those who say that the butter and so on of creatures whose meat is not allowable are also not allowable, speak without knowledge. The mention of butter and so on of creatures whose meat is allowable is intended to show the limit of the forfeiture (nissaggiya) object, which may be used for seven days and must be forfeited after seven days. Similarly, in the Paṇītabhojanasikkhāpada, it is stated to show that only the milk and so on of creatures whose meat is allowable are considered superior food (paṇītabhojana), and not others. It is also written that honey (madhu) refers to "great honey" (mahamadhu) which is like resin in the nests of honeybees, carpenter bees, and flies, and it is a life-long medicine (yāvajīvika).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Medicines (Bhesajjasikkhāpada) is finished.

## The Third Chapter, the Bowl Chapter (Pattavagga), is finished.

## The Explanation of the Forfeiture and Expiation (Nissaggiya Pācittiya) is finished.
89: ## Pācittiyakaṇḍa  ## 4. Bhojanavagga  ## 2. Gaṇabhojana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā  Devadatta, being with a group, requested and ate food in the morning. Because of that requesting and eating with a group, the Blessed One prescribed the Gaṇabhojana training rule: "There is a Pācittiya offense for a group meal." In the Padabhājanī of the Pali text, it is analyzed by taking only "invitation," stating "being invited, they eat." However, in the Andhaka Commentary, it is written that "requesting by means of intimation (viññatti)" is also taught based on the story. Why? Because in the Parivāra Pali itself, it is taught: "A group meal arises in two ways: from requesting or from [improper] invitation." Therefore, it should be understood that it was not taught in the Padabhājanī because eating by requesting is already clear in the origin (aṭṭhuppatti) of the training rule.  In this passage, "they receive together" means that even monks who have already received alms-food are considered to be "receiving together" if they remain within the twelve-cubit precinct (upacāra) without leaving as long as other monks are still receiving. "Any monk" refers to any of the five fellow-dhamma practitioners or to the titthiyas (ascetics of other sects). "Absence of occasion" means the absence of the seven occasions where there is no offense. "Together with the monk who has obtained an occasion, they become a group of four." "The monk who has obtained an occasion is himself free from the Gaṇabhojana Pācittiya offense, but for the remaining three monks, he is one who causes an offense because he completes the group." This is what is written.  Here, an objector asks: "It has been said that 'receiving' alone is the measure here. If so, why is it taught in the Pali text: 'A group meal means where four monks... eat'?" The answer to this is: In that statement, "they eat" is a word that marks "receiving." Indeed, monks do not eat food that has not been formally offered.  ## Gaṇabhojana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā is finished.  ## 3. Paramparabhojana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā  In this context of "except on occasion," some teachers say that a Pācittiya offense occurs for eating with regard to causing an out-of-turn meal (paramparabhojana) or due to an improper invitation. A monk, while wandering for alms, receives food. Another lay devotee invites him with an improper invitation and has him sit in the house, but that food...
90: is completed. If that monk eats the food he obtained while wandering for alms, he commits an offense. Why? Because it is taught: "An out-of-turn meal (paramparabhojana) means being invited for one of the five [types of] food, setting that aside, and eating another of the five foods; this is called an out-of-turn meal." The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to the first Kathina training rule. It is stated in the commentary that this training rule is kiriyākiriya (action and non-action).  ## Paramparabhojana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā is finished.  ## 4. Kāṇamātā Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā  "Two or three bowlfuls may be accepted" means that a monk who desires the cakes brought in that manner should accept them according to the measure of a superior (ukkaṭṭha) bowl. If one does not inform [another monk], "Venerable sir, do not accept here," or if one accepts in excess not for the sake of travel provisions, or if one does not share, one is not free from the offense. This is because this training rule is acittaka (an offense incurred regardless of intention). If one takes what is not formally offered (uggahitaka), one is certainly not free from the offense. However, in the case of not sharing, there is no offense if the item is unallowable (akappiya). Some teachers say, "It is acittaka only through not knowing the regulation (paṇṇatti), not through not knowing the object (vatthu)." Since "not knowing it was prepared for travel provisions" is not mentioned among the factors, ancient teachers say that if one intentionally does not speak [to warn another], a Pācittiya offense is incurred. In the term "accepting in excess," only the fifth factor is shown; therefore, as long as one has not yet accepted [more than three bowls], a Pācittiya is not yet incurred, but a dukkhaṭa (offense of wrong-doing) is incurred for not doing what should be done (i.e., not preventing). Otherwise, this training rule would become kiriyākiriya. Not preventing or not informing should be stated as the sixth factor.  ## Kāṇamātā Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā is finished.  ## 5. Paṭhamapavāraṇā Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā  The refusal of food (pavāraṇā) by one who has finished eating has five factors. Among those factors, since "having finished eating" is established by the factor "food is evident," no separate distinct meaning is seen. It is written in the Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā that if they are taken separately, it would show six factors. "Food is evident" is said with reference to food that has been brought into one's presence.
91:
In the phrase 'powder made by pounding,' the word 'pi' (also) includes broken rice (kuṇḍaka). Since it is mentioned that only broken rice or any kind of rice from paddy that is moderately roasted or dried in the sun is intended, the rice powder from moderately roasted paddy or from empty grains of paddy triggers the refusal (pavāraṇā). Similarly, broken rice that is well-roasted also triggers the refusal. It is written that uncooked modaka cakes (laḍḍu) made by balling together roasted flour also trigger the refusal. If there is no remaining food, it does not trigger the refusal. Why? Because there is no unfinished meal known as 'eating.'

Although unallowable meat is in a state that should be rejected, it does not lose its nature as meat when being chewed; therefore, (rejecting it while chewing) triggers the refusal. If one rejects a portion that has not yet reached them while eating in the dining hall, it does not trigger the refusal. Even if one rejects it, if the monastery attendants (ārāmika) pour it into the bowl, it is not allowable to eat that food. This is because such food is regarded as being obtained through wrong livelihood (anesanā), which is loathed by the Buddha. Just as it should be understood that the refusal is not triggered if one rejects alms-food given by an immoral monk from the Saṅgha's portion, so too is the completeness of this example. However, if one rejects food given by a conscientious (lajjī) monk because of a lack of desire to swallow it, it triggers the refusal. If one rejects when offered 'meat juice' (mamsarasa), it triggers the refusal. This is because it implies 'juice together with meat.' The teacher Vajirabuddhi states that the grammatical derivation (vigga-ha) 'juice of meat' is not intended here.

If one brings gruel mixed with boiled rice and says, 'Please take the gruel,' rejecting it does not trigger the refusal. If one says, 'Please take the boiled rice,' rejecting it triggers the refusal. Why? Because that boiled rice food is present. In this context, if one says, 'Please take the food mixed with gruel,' and the gruel is more or equal (and the rice is less), rejecting it does not trigger the refusal. If the gruel is less and the boiled rice is more, rejecting it triggers the refusal. Since this is stated in all the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), it should not be rejected, though the reason here is difficult to see. If one says, 'Please take the food mixed with boiled rice,' whether the rice is more, equal, or less, rejecting it definitely triggers the refusal. If one says, 'Please take the mixture,' without naming it as boiled rice or gruel, if the rice is more or equal, rejecting it triggers the refusal. If the rice is less, it does not trigger the refusal. All of this should be carefully investigated.
92:
Regarding fruits or roots, etc., that have not yet been made allowable by the five kinds of monastic procedures (samaṇakappa): In this case, if fruits like bananas that have not been made allowable are mixed in the bowl, one may set aside those bananas and eat the remaining fruits, whether or not the excess-food procedure (atirikta-vinayakamma) is performed. Since they are fruits with non-mixing juices, one should have those bananas made allowable again, place them in another vessel, perform the excess-food procedure, and then eat them. Why? Because it is said that the Vinaya procedure of making them allowable had not yet been applied to those new fruits.

Dust falling into the bowl is considered not yet accepted. Therefore, one should continue to receive alms-food only after accepting it. Because it is said, 'For a monk who takes without accepting, there is a Dukkaṭa offense according to the Vinaya,' this practice is also not allowable for other monks. In the statement 'There is no offense for one who eats that alms-food after accepting it again,' it is the same. In this First Pavāraṇā training rule, regarding the factor 'made into excess food, not made into excess food,' the decision on what is allowable or not should be known by investigating these factors.

'This is all enough' means 'This food is also in excess for you; you will not receive any other food besides this.' 'For the sake of nutriment' means only at the wrong time (after noon), according to some teachers. There is also a reading: 'They are like the first Kathina; this is an action or non-action.' It should be understood that a bodily act (kāyakamma) occurs through swallowing, and a verbal act (vacīkamma) occurs by not having someone perform the procedure with the words, 'Venerable sir, please make this excess food.'

## End of the Commentary on the First Pavāraṇā Training Rule.

## 6. Dutiya-pavāraṇā-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

Because it is stated in the Matika, 'A Pācittiya offense when eaten,' it is said that 'A Pācittiya offense is incurred at the end of the meal,' not with every swallow.

## End of the Commentary on the Second Pavāraṇā Training Rule.
93:
## 7. Vikālabhojana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
It is heard that the time is demarcated according to the time in Jambudīpa.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Eating at the Wrong Time is finished.

## 8. Sannidhikāraka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
## Because it is stated in this Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary in the manner beginning with "it is poorly washed," and because it is stated in the Samantapāsādikā (Pācittiya Commentary 253), "After washing a poorly washed bowl, one should pour clear water into that bowl again, or rub it with a finger to know the state of being free from grease," it is written as established that the grease absorbed by the shard (or crack) of a clay bowl constitutes storing up (sannidhi).

In the statement "having accepted it oneself and not relinquished it," "not relinquished" (appaccatta) means not giving away or not abandoning without concern for the novices, thinking "I will eat it later." Elder Dhammasiri said, "In this matter of acceptance, only the non-relinquishment of the state of being accepted produces storing up (sannidhi)." That statement contradicts the Pāḷi text, "He accepts it; there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa)" (Pācittiya 255). However, since there is no need to accept that stored food again, it should be investigated and reflected upon.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Storing Up Food is finished.

## 9. Paṇီtabhojana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
"The meat, milk, and curd of those animals are intended here"—this statement is the demarcation of the physical basis (vatthu) for the Pācittiya offense, but it is not the demarcation of allowable milk and so on. Therefore, the milk and so on of any unspecified animal are allowable. Furthermore, if one requests the group of five medicines such as ghee for the sake of medicine when invited by the power of the Saṅgha, as in "it should be done by the Mahānāma training rule," it is included in this Pāḷi text: "One should not request medicine when there is no need for medicine." Therefore, it is written, "By that [request], there is a Pācittiya offense" (Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā, Pācittiya 261).

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Superior Food is finished.
94:
## 10. Dantapona Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
Because it is said "with a part of the body," receiving with the mouth is permitted. It is written that "it is not allowable to receive on leaves such as tamarind leaves spread on the ground; it is allowable only in a suitable time/region (kalla-khetta) for that receiving." Also, by the words "having taken it oneself," it is not only for a snake bite, but even if bitten by another creature, it is allowable to take it oneself and consume it.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Tooth-sticks is finished.

## 5. Acelakavagga

## 1. Acelaka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In this Acelaka training rule, since those such as the naked ones are known only as titthiyas (sectarians),
Therefore, the triad-demarcation was made by the name titthiya.
The decision is that it is allowable to give to a naked person who is not a titthiya, and likewise to a layperson or a monk who has the appearance of a titthiya.
It is our view that it is allowable to give to persons such as Stream-enterers (sotāpanna) who have the appearance of a titthiya, with the thought that they are not titthiyas.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Naked Ascetics is finished.

## 3. Sabhojana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
The state of having one's own intention should be known by the intention of entering near and wanting to sit.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Eating Together is finished.

## 4-5. Rahopaṭicchanna-Rahonisajja Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
The fourth training rule is in the same manner as stated in the first Aniyata, and the fifth training rule is in the same manner as stated in the second Aniyata. In this chapter, the fifth training rule is the fourth for Venerable Upananda.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Sitting in Private is finished.
95:
## 6. Cāritta Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the text "sabhatto samāno," the ancient teachers say it means "one who has an invited meal." There are four supplementary regulations (anupaññatti) in this Cāritta training rule: the regulation on "not informing a monk who is present," the regulation on "before the meal," the regulation on "after the meal," and the regulation on "except on [certain] occasions." Among those, "occasions" (samaya) are of two kinds: the time of giving robes and the time of making robes. "Bhattiyaghara" refers to the house of the donor who gave the invitation or the house of the donors who will give ticket-food (salākabhatta) and so on. There is a commentary text: "The origin (samuṭṭhāna) and so on are similar to the first Kathina training rule, but this training rule is an act of commission or omission (kiriyā-akiriya)." Some teachers say, "In this Cāritta training rule, the invitation is an unallowable invitation."

If a monk, before eating the invited meal, wanders for alms and eats the alms-food obtained, he would commit a Pācittiya offense of pāramparabhojana (consecutive meals); if he eats after eating the invited meal, that offense would not occur.

Even after eating the invited meal, if a monk who is about to go on a journey goes to a previous house, some teachers say there is an offense, while others say there is no offense.

Other teachers who hold the view that there is an offense in this training rule say that because of having expectations for the same meal, there is an offense in entering another family's house.

It should be known that when inviting that monk, they go with a group-meal (gaṇabhatta); some teachers say that eating at that time is equal in terms of offense, while others say that the presence of the monk who should be informed is evident.

Only those monks who desire a decision, through the divisions to be investigated, know this training rule as the Cāritta training rule, as shown by the wise (Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā, Pācittiya 294).

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Visiting is finished.

## 7. Mahānāma Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
The meaning of the words "it should be done by the Mahānāma training rule" in the Paṇītabhojana training rule is that if one requests the five medicines such as ghee for the sake of medicine when invited by the power of the Saṅgha, it is written that a Pācittiya offense occurs by the words "one requests medicine when there is no need for medicine." Only a sick monk (gilāna) gets to request by speaking truthfully, "You, donor, have invited with only this medicine; we have a need for this and that medicine," but another who is not sick (agilāna) does not. And for the sake of another sick monk...
96:
The meaning of the word "for the benefit of another" is (requesting) from the relatives or those who have invited that sick monk, or from one's own relatives or those who have invited. "One who is invited with an unlimited invitation" refers to donors who have invited by way of the Saṅgha or by way of an individual. Therefore, although it is said "inviting the Saṅgha," it is not said "inviting an individual." Since a sick monk is already included by the phrase "exceeding the limit," it is not specifically mentioned as "being sick or not sick." Even so, since it is found written in the commentary text as "inviting by way of inviting the Saṅgha," it should be investigated and reflected upon.

## Conclusion of Mahānāma Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā.

## 8. Uyyuttasenā Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
"Each one" among elephants and so on means, at the minimum, even an elephant ridden by a single man, or a single man holding an arrow in his hand (referring to going to see them). The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so on are similar to the Eḷakaloma Sikkhāpada. This training rule, however, is a worldly fault (lokavajja); there is a text stating it arises with an unwholesome mind and is associated with the three feelings.

## Conclusion of Uyyuttasenā Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā.

## 9. Senāvāsa Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
"Blocked by someone" means being blocked by someone such as an enemy or a ruler like a king. The boundary of the army's location should be defined by the army's enclosure such as a wall, or by a place suitable for an enclosure, or by the limit of the area where the soldiers move about.

## Conclusion of Senāvāsa Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā.

## The Fifth: Acelaka Vagga.

## 6. Surāpāna Vagga

## 1. Surāpāna Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
It is written that in drinking while knowing it is "liquor" or that "it is not allowable," there is only an unwholesome mind. It is said that the phrase "unwholesome mind" is mostly stated with reference to that unwholesome mind alone. Furthermore,
97:
If it is asked, "Why is it stated in the Vinaya Commentary, 'Because it should be drunk only with an unwholesome mind (it is an unwholesome mind)'?" It is stated because, in the aspect of being intentional (sacittaka), it is drunk only with an unwholesome mind.

## Conclusion of Surāpāna Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā.

## 2. Aṅgulipatodaka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
Although the nature of the Saṅghādisesa offense of physical contact is the same, a Dukkaṭa offense occurs (if touched) in the case of a nun or an unordained person (anupasampanna), but a Pācittiya offense occurs only in the case of an ordained monk (upasampanna); thus, to show the regard for the person, it was taught: "There is a Pācittiya offense in tickling with fingers (aṅgulipatodaka)." In this text, "when there is a duty to be done," the meaning is (no offense) for a monk who touches a man when there is a duty to be done, not (for touching) a woman.

## Conclusion of Aṅgulipatodaka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā.

## 3. Hasadhamma Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
Because of the words "or mud," there is only a Dukkaṭa offense for a monk who plays by throwing even a pebble. It is stated as "a Pācittiya offense due to sporting in water (hasadhamma)" by virtue of the object of the Pācittiya offense, which is a Pācittiya offense above the ankle and a Dukkaṭa offense elsewhere.

If this Hasadhamma Sikkhāpada is a release through perception (saññāvimokkha), (if so) how can there be a triad of Pācittiya (tika-pācittiya)? That offense would occur by wrongly perceiving playing itself as not playing.

To what extent is it playing? In this playing itself, there is one who has the perception of it not being playing; in this matter, one should undertake the meaning of the Vinaya.

Since the mind that delights in playing is certainly unwholesome, therefore, only one kind of unwholesome mind is obtained in this matter. (Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā, Pācittiya, 336).

## Conclusion of Hasadhamma Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā.
98:
## 4. Anādariya Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
"Tassa vacanaṃ" means one acts with disrespect, thinking, "This monk is one who has been expelled, or one who is blamed, or one who is censured; his words will not be followed (will not amount to being heard)." "Dhammaṃ" means one acts with disrespect, either by thinking, "How might this Dhamma disappear, or be destroyed, or vanish?" or by not wishing to train in that training rule. It is written in the Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā: "It is not allowable for a monk who, having transgressed a worldly fault (lokavajja), says, 'This view is the one learned by our teachers'."

## Conclusion of Anādariya Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā.

## 6. Joti Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
Because it is taught in the training rule as "expecting to warm oneself (visibbanāpekkho)," it is allowable for the sake of another person, or for the sake of many others.

Monks kindle a single fire or many fires together with firewood and so on. Due to the specific intention of the Buddha, one group of monks extinguishes the fire (does not burn), while many groups of monks do not extinguish the fire (they burn).

## Conclusion of Joti Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā.

## 8. Dubbaṇṇakaraṇa Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
"Morakkhimaṇḍalamaṅgulapiṭṭhīnaṃ": these measurements are not absolute. They say it is allowable whether it is larger or smaller than the size of a peacock's eye-circle or a bedbug's back. Even at a single corner of the robe, thus, making even a single smudge-mark (kappabindu) anywhere on the robe is allowable.

## Conclusion of Dubbaṇṇakaraṇa Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā.

## 9. Vikappana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
There is a text: "The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so on are similar to the first Kathina Sikkhāpada; this training rule, however, is action and non-action (kiriyā-akiriya)." In this training rule, using (a robe that has not yet been assigned back) is a bodily action. Not withdrawing (not returning the assignment) is a vocal action.

## Conclusion of Vikappana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā.
99:
## 10. Apanidhāna-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
Ancient teachers stated that for a monk who hides or causes to be hidden a needle-case together with a needle, Pācittiya offenses are incurred according to the number of needles.

## The Commentary on the Apanidhāna Training Rule is finished.

## The Sixth Chapter, the Surāpāna-vagga, is finished.

## 7. Sappāṇaka-vagga

## 1. Sañcicca-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
The count of karmic bondage (kammabandha) occurs according to the count of the objects, which are the living beings one kills. Among the karmic bondage and the intentions to kill, the intentions to kill occur according to the count of karmic bondage. In this act of killing, it should be understood through this analysis that many animals die through a single intention.

## The Commentary on the Sañcicca Training Rule is finished.

## 2. Sappāṇaka-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
Regarding "Sappāṇaka" (containing living beings), a Pācittiya is incurred by way of the death of the insects, not by way of using water containing insects. For this very reason, it is called a "prohibited fault" (paṇṇatti-vajja). A Pācittiya is incurred due to having an impure mind; if the mind is pure, there is no offense. It is written that its status as a prohibited fault is stated as in the case of lighting a lamp.

Putting [grass or clay] into water was the former [rule],
Entering water is this [rule];
Thus, the difference between these two [rules]
Should always be known by the wise.

## The Commentary on the Sappāṇaka Training Rule is finished.

## 5. Ūnavīsativassa-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
Regarding "ordains another":

If the preceptor (upajjhāya) himself performs the ordination and also recites the kammavācā,
some teachers say the act is successful.
The expert in Vinaya says the act is not successful.
100:
Because the Blessed One has prescribed a dukkaṭa offense for both the teacher (ācariya) and the group (gaṇa). Therefore, in this ordination, the teacher and the preceptor are indeed distinct and separate.

## The Commentary on the Ūnavīsativassa Training Rule is finished.

## 7. Saṃvidhāna-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
In this Saṃvidhāna training rule, these three—the bhikkhunī ordained on one side (ekato-upasampannā), the female trainee (sikkhamānā), and the female novice (sāmaṇerī)—are also included. Specifically, for these three, the time mentioned in the Saṃvidhāna training rule of the Ovāda-vagga protects them. This should be understood as the distinction between these three and women who are not fellow practitioners.

## The Commentary on the Saṃvidhāna Training Rule is finished.

## 9. Ukkhittasambhoga-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
"With one who has not relinquished that view" is written with reference to a monk of a different communion due to his views (laddhi-nānāsaṃvāsaka). In this commentary phrase "three types of mind," the meaning should be understood as: "one might lie down together with that expelled monk with a resultant indeterminate mind (vipāka-abyākata-citta)." Otherwise, since this training rule is one involving intention (sacittaka), it is not appropriate to refer to a functional indeterminate mind (kiriya-abyākata-citta).

## The Commentary on the Ukkhittasambhoga Training Rule is finished.

## 10. Kaṇṭaka-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
"This novice is one who has committed a Pārājika; if he relinquishes that view, he should be expelled with the permission of the Saṅgha after informing the Saṅgha"—so it is said in the ancient Gaṇṭhipada. That statement is not appropriate. Because in this Kaṇṭaka training rule, destruction by punishment (daṇḍakamma-nāsanā) is intended. If that novice were one who committed a Pārājika, it would be called destruction of the outward form (liṅga-nāsanā). The view "indulging in those sensual pleasures is not able to cause an obstacle" is not the kind of view that considers the Teacher (the Buddha) as not being the Teacher. If that view arises in someone, that person becomes a Pārājika-offender; in that person also...
101: ...one should proceed in the same way; a novice who does not remain in restraint should be destroyed by the destruction of the outward form (liṅga-nāsanā)—this is the teacher's opinion. ## The Commentary on the Kaṇṭaka Training Rule is finished. ## The Seventh Chapter, the Sappāṇaka-vagga. ## 8. Sahadhammika-vagga ## 4. Pahāra-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā If it is asked: "Among the factors of the Pahāra training rule, just as the absence of the desire to be released is mentioned, should the absence of the desire for death also be mentioned?" It should not be mentioned. Why? Because a monk who himself wishes to give a blow, thinking that there is simply an absence of effort toward that person's death by his intention, and because it is a matter related to non-death, he merely has no desire for death; therefore, unlike the desire for release, the absence of the desire for death is not included. For one who has the desire for release, there is no anger; therefore, it is taught that there is no offense. ## The Commentary on the Pahāra Training Rule is finished. ## 5. Talasattika-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā The palm itself is called "talasattika." Some teachers say, "It is called 'sattika' in the sense of being capable of striking." For a monk who strikes with the desire to strike, a Pācittiya is incurred by the previous Pahāra training rule. If he merely makes a gesture of raising [the hand] with the desire to threaten, a Pācittiya is incurred by this Talasattika training rule. If, deviating from this training rule, a blow is given, a dukkaṭa is incurred because it was not given with the desire to strike [as defined in the previous rule]. Is this dukkaṭa due to the striking or due to the raising? The dukkaṭa is due to the striking only; the Pācittiya is due to the previous raising. Thus, a Pācittiya together with a dukkaṭa is appropriate. Indeed, the raising occurs first and the striking occurs later. The teacher says: "It is our opinion that the previous raising cannot become a non-offense based on the subsequent striking." ## The Commentary on the Talasattika Training Rule is finished.
102:
## 7. Sañcicca Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
Whether the other person develops remorse or not is not the criterion. It should be understood that the third factor, "causing remorse," is stated according to the intention of that monk.

## The Commentary on the Sañcicca Training Rule is finished.

## 8. Upassuti Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
Regarding "upassuti" (eavesdropping), just as "upakujjha" is said to mean "crouching nearby (samīpakujjha)," so too "upassuti" should be understood as "listening nearby (samīpassuti)." It refers to the place where one stands and hears. In this context, "suti" also refers to the sound of others' speech. It is called "suti" because it is heard. Alternatively, it is called "upassuti" because it is heard in that place. The place itself is also called "suti." In the phrase "having heard [the speech] of these people," the word "speech (vacanaṃ)" is an elided term.

The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth of this training rule should not be taken as being the same as the previous two training rules. It is of the theyyasattha-samuṭṭhāna (originating like the theft of a caravan). It can be an action (kiriya) by going to listen. It can also be an inaction (akiriya) by staying in one's place and not letting the speakers know of one's presence. It is recorded as: "saññāvimokkha, sacittaka, lokavajja, kāyakamma, vacīkamma, akusala-citta, dukkhavedanā."

## The Commentary on the Upassuti Training Rule is finished.

## 9. Kammapappaṭibāhana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
The monk who is the assigner of minor items (appamattakavissajjaka) may give various items such as needles, which are mentioned in the commentary on the Senāsanakkhandhaka (Cullavagga, 328), to a monk making robes even without asking the Saṅgha. If he wishes to give more than that, he must perform the act of obtaining leave (apalokana-kamma). The meaning is that such an act of obtaining leave is merely a characteristic of the formal act (kammalakkhaṇa). Thus, the kammalakkhaṇa should be understood in all cases. Formal acts of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma) such as restoration (osāraṇā) in village boundaries and monasteries are not allowable. However, giving items that are to be distributed or divided is allowable. It is recorded that one should not say generally "this is the property of the Saṅgha," but should specifically obtain leave by saying, "this is the property of the Saṅgha in this monastery." It is also recorded that "the origins and so forth are similar to taking what is not given (adinnādāna), but this training rule involves painful feeling (dukkhavedanā)."

## The Commentary on the Kammapappaṭibāhana Training Rule is finished.
103:
## 10. Chandamadatvāgamana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
Some teachers say that if one does not come to the assembly and does not give consent (chanda), there is no offense. Other teachers say that a dukkaṭa offense is incurred because there is an intention to obstruct a legal act (dhamma-kamma).

## The Commentary on the Chandamadatvāgamana Training Rule is finished.

## 11. Dubbala Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
"Akappaṭiyena vā" (or with what is unallowable) refers to things such as couches or beds made of gold or silver. "An allowable couch should be accepted" is said in reference to a couch given with the words "we give this to the Saṅgha." However, if the donors say "we give this to the monastery," then even unallowable couches made of gold, silver, and so forth may be accepted. It is also recorded that "arañjara refers to a large water jar that holds much water." Regarding "saṅghikapābhogena vā," it means that if monastery attendants and others store it and then return it, it is allowable to use. It is recorded that "even if a vessel made of bronze, copper, etc., is given to the Saṅgha, it is not allowable to carry it around wherever one goes," as stated in the Samantapāsādikā; therefore, one is not permitted to take it with one's own hand to store it. It is also recorded that "vedaka refers to a waistband ring," and that there is a text: "hiṅgu, hiṅguli, haritāla, manosilā, añjanāni." Furthermore, there is a text: "dārumayo vā... even a casket without feet," and "dārumayo tumbo refers to a wooden water-bottle," and "in pillars, beams, rafters, stairs, floorboards, and so forth."

## The Commentary on the Dubbala Training Rule is finished.

## 12. Pariṇāmana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
A monk wishes to give a gift to a suspended (ukkhittaka) monk; if one prevents that gift and makes him give it to another, there is no offense. Likewise, if one makes a person give to another by preventing the gift of one who is diverting faith-offerings, there is no offense. If one's own pupils wish to give a bowl to a certain person and ask for permission, and one says, "This person is incompatible (visabhāga), give it to a compatible one (sabhāga)," there is no offense because it is one's own responsibility. However, if that pupil wishes to give to a compatible person and one makes him give to another...
104:
...if one makes them give to another (compatible person), it is indeed an offense. In all matters of property, one has the right to manage as one pleases a pupil who wishes to give after having asked for permission.

## The Commentary on the Pariṇāmana Training Rule is finished.

## The Eighth Chapter, the Sahadhammika Vagga, is finished.

## 9. Ratana Vagga

## 1. Antepura Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
"Asayanighara" (sleeping chamber) refers to places such as the foot of a tree which are outside the enclosure. The teacher says, "If he is a Khattiya but has not yet been consecrated, or if he is consecrated but is not a Khattiya, it protects (from an offense)." This is because "being a Khattiya" and "being consecrated" are stated as factors for the offense. The origins and so forth are similar to the first Kathina training rule, but there is a text stating that this training rule is "kiriākiriā" (action-inaction).

## The Commentary on the Antepura Training Rule is finished.

## 2. Ratana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
The entire course of the discussion proceeds by excluding the act of taking and guarding (valuables) under the heading of being a treasurer (bhaṇḍāgārika).

## The Commentary on the Ratana Training Rule is finished.

## 3. Vikālagāmappavesana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
There is a text stating that "santā bhikkhuṃ," "anāpucchā," and "tathārūpā accāyikā" are the three (factors/amendments) in this rule. The origins and so forth are similar to the Kathina training rule, but there is a text stating that this training rule is "kiriākiriā."

## The Commentary on the Vikālagāmappavesana Training Rule is finished.
105:
## 4. Commentary on the Sūcighara Training Rule
"Taṃ assa" means that since it should be confessed after first breaking it, that breaking belongs to that Pācittiya offense. This method is the same in other training rules as well. "Vāsijaṭe" means in the handle of a hatchet.

## The Commentary on the Sūcighara Training Rule is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Mañcapīṭha Training Rule
"Aṭṭhaṅgulapādakaṃ" is a neuter noun used adverbially (bhāvanapuṃsaka). Placing it on the crossbeams is indeed the making of a scaffold.

## The Commentary on the Mañcapīṭha Training Rule is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Tūlonaddha Training Rule
Even if it appears as if a Pācittiya offense occurs at the very time of acquisition, in reality, the offense should be understood to occur only at the time of use. The statement "If one acquires and uses what was made by another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" is the evidence here.

## The Commentary on the Tūlonaddha Training Rule is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Nisīdana Training Rule
Although the specific type (jāti) of the sitting cloth (nisīdana) is not seen in this training rule, it should be known that its type is just a type of robe (cīvara), because it is allowed in the Cīvarakkhandhaka and because it is included in the statement "Nine robes should be determined (adhiṭṭhāna)." Although some teachers say, "If available, a sitting cloth with a border is allowable; if not, even one without a border is allowable," that statement is not appropriate. This is because the shape of the sitting cloth is defined by the statement, "What is called a sitting cloth is said to have a border."

## The Commentary on the Nisīdana Training Rule is finished.

## The Ninth Chapter, the Ratana Vagga.

## The Commentary on the Suddhapācittiya is finished.

## The Section on Pāṭidesanīya
## 1. Commentary on the First Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule
Regarding Yāmakālika etc., if taken for the sake of nutriment, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). That dukkaṭa offense occurs in the taste of Yāmakālika, Sattāhakālika, and Yāvajīvika that is not mixed with food (āmisa) such as alms-food. However, if mixed with food such as alms-food and having a single taste (the combination of the three types of kālika), there is only a Pāṭidesanīya offense for the monk who receives it.

## The Commentary on the First Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule is finished.
## 2. Commentary on the Second Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule
There is a passage in the Commentary: "The origin (samuṭṭhāna) etc. are similar to the Kathina training rule, but this training rule is kariyākariya (action and non-action)."

## The Commentary on the Second Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule is finished.
## 4. Commentary on the Fourth Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule
"For a monk who, having received it in a monastery or the vicinity of a monastery, eats it" means for a monk who, having received it in a monastery or its vicinity, eats it in a monastery or its vicinity.

There is no offense for a monk who eats inside a monastery food that was received outside the monastery. Among the factors for an offense, "receiving inside a monastery or its vicinity" should be taken. This is because when the interior of the monastery is shown, the vicinity of the monastery is already shown. There is a passage in the Commentary: "The origin etc. are similar to the Kathina training rule, but this training rule is kariyākariya."

## The Commentary on the Fourth Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule is finished.
## The Commentary on the Pāṭidesanīya is finished.
107:
## The Section on Sekhiya
Although there is a transgression in the Sekhiya training rules, the person (agent) was not mentioned to show that the offense is only for one who disregards out of disrespect. This is the nature of the Vinaya: where there is disregard, the agent is indicated, which is the rule in the stated regulation, and the use of the locative and instrumental cases. It is allowable to wear the lower robe even lower than eight finger-breadths below the knee. It is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā that there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for a monk who wears it lower than that. "Ārāme vā" refers to times such as attending upon the Buddha. The word "pārupitabbaṃ" (should be robed) is said by way of the duty of the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga).

Regarding "ṭhatvā" (standing), it is written in the Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā that even while walking, one is allowed to look around to see if there is no danger. Just as a monk staying overnight is allowed to sit with his body uncovered inside a house, so a monk wishing to go to that monk is allowed to go as he pleases without tying the waist-band, without wearing the outer robe, and without announcing the village-entry duty. Therefore, while traveling a long distance, if one monk fulfills the village-entry duty, enters the village, reaches a rest house in front, puts down his requisites, and stays there, other monks are allowed to go to that monk comfortably. What need is there to mention going to monks who have resolved to stay for four or five days, or going to monks who stay for a long time? One is also allowed to go comfortably to a Buddha-pūjā. It is also said in the Commentary: "One looks here and there depending on a reason." It is written that the "reason" there should be understood as material offerings (āmisa-pūjā).

## The Commentary on the Twenty-six Sāruppa is finished.

"Alms-food equal to the rim of the bowl should be received" shows that alms-food filled up to the rim should be received; therefore, it implies that it is allowable even if the alms-food poured into the bowl in one's hand is heaped up. In eating bean-curry and alms-food by requesting it, if after putting it in the mouth one feels regret and wishes to spit it out, but it goes down quickly, it is called "eating unintentionally (asañcicca bhuñjati)." If one quickly takes and eats requested alms-food and non-requested alms-food that are in the same place without reflecting, it is called "eating unmindfully (assatiyā bhuñjati)."

There is a passage: "The Sūpodanavinnatti training rule has an origin similar to the caravan-of-thieves rule, it is kariya, it is saññāvimokkha, it is sacittaka, it is lokavajja, it is kāyakamma and vacīkamma, it has unwholesome consciousness, and it has painful feeling."

## Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha
## Homage to Him, the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One
## The Chapter on Defeat (Pārājika-kaṇḍa)

Regarding the term "abhilāpamattameva" (merely a mode of address): In the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha, there are two types of address—"Bhante" according to junior status and "Āvuso" according to senior status. However, in this Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha, there is only one mode of address for both seniors and juniors, which is "Ayyā."

Regarding the phrase "kāyasaṃsagge vuttanayena" (by the method stated in the bodily contact [rule]): Here, the state of being action-originated (kiriya-samuṭṭhāna) is stated according to the general rule (tabbahula-naya). In fact, because it is not preached as "should fall into bodily contact" (kāyasaṃsanggaṃ samāpajjeyya) but as "should consent" (sādiyeyya), it should be understood that the offense also arises through non-action (akiriya), such as passive acquiescence. Just as in this (Ubbajāṇumaṇḍalikā) training rule, in the First Pārājika training rule below, it is first preached as action-originated by the method: "For a monk who indulges in sexual intercourse in the three paths of a human woman, there is an offense of Defeat." Immediately after that, it is also preached as non-action-originated by the method: "The enemies of a monk bring a human woman to the monk and insert the male organ into the excrementary path; if that monk consents to the insertion..." Therefore, it should be understood that in the First Pārājika as well, it is action-originated only according to the general rule. This is because the state of being action-originated is not found in instances such as consenting to insertion.

In this First Pārājika account, the movement of the male organ should not be taken as the essence. Why? Because in the passage: "If that monk does not consent to the insertion, does not consent to it once inserted, does not consent while it is stationary, but consents to the withdrawal, there is an offense of Defeat," there is full movement even in the state of not consenting while stationary. Since the movement related to indulgence due to consent is not seen here, it should be taken as action-originated only by the general rule.

In another way, because that consent (or action-origination) is preached in its specific form in the Bhikkhunī's First Pārājika, it is stated as "action-originated" in accordance with that Matika, without looking at the method of the Vibhaṅga. Just as it is stated in these training rules that they are action-originated by the general rule, likewise, the drinking of intoxicants and so forth must be done only with an unwholesome mind. Otherwise, "Whosoever...
110:
"One falls into an offense only with an unwholesome mind; this offense is called a worldly fault (lokavajja), while the remaining offenses are called prescribed faults (paṇṇattivajja)." If it is stated this way, the defining characteristic of worldly and prescribed faults is established. If it were stated (as in the Kaṅkhā-vitaranī Commentary): "In the intentional (sacittaka) aspect of an offense, the mind is only unwholesome; this offense is called a worldly fault, while the remaining are prescribed faults," then the term 'worldly fault' would be useless, because even in the aspect of not knowing the object, one would still be drinking with an unwholesome mind.

Because in the case of not knowing the object, there is no arising of an unwholesome mind in the transgression of drinking intoxicants. Therefore, it is stated in the Khandhaka Commentary: "Regarding the drinking of intoxicants, if a monk drinks intoxicants starting from the seed (stage) without knowing, there is an offense of pācittiya. A novice (sāmaṇera) reaches a breach of virtue only if he drinks knowingly; he does not if he drinks unknowingly." It is not stated: "Even if there is an arising of mind similar to the unwholesome mind that completes [the act of] killing and so forth in the aspect of not knowing the object, the novice does not breach his virtue." The statement regarding firm conviction is because the drinking of intoxicants by novices follows the same course as killing and so forth. For one who transgresses by drinking, etc., while knowing the object as "these are intoxicants," there is no absence of unwholesome [intent]. Therefore, it is said: "In the intentional aspect of an offense..." and so forth.

In this matter—if it is asked: "What is the use of defining it as unwholesome in both intentional and unintentional aspects, since intoxicants do not enter [the mouths of] Arahants by way of logic?"—it is not so, because by way of nature (dhammatā), they do not enter [the mouths of] learners (sekha) either. To show the absence of the unwholesome definition in the unintentional aspect, examples such as drops of intoxicants should be given, like drops of water placed in the mouth of a sleeping person. Indeed, if the meaning is taken by the general rule, the preceding and following words agree with the Commentary and the Pali. The teachers also say that there is no unwholesome definition in drinking intoxicants. 

Some teachers, however, say that the action-origination of that drinking of intoxicants is only by the general rule, but not in the First Pārājika. How? The training rule on bodily contact (kāyasaṃsangga) has the same origination as the First Pārājika. In this matter, when there is bodily contact between a monk and a bhikkhunī, the bhikkhunī falls into an offense even if she does not move her limbs but merely consents and accepts with her mind; the monk is not like that. A monk falls into an offense only if he moves. In the same way, in the First Pārājika, one falls into an offense only if there is movement; if there is none, one does not. In the phrase "consents to the insertion" (pavesanaṃ sādiyati), what is called 'consenting to insertion' is the arising of the mind to indulge, or they desire the entry of the [male] organ into the [female] organ. For such a person, bodily movement certainly exists. Even so, it is written that it should be taken after careful consideration.

## The Commentary on the Pārājika is finished.
111:
## Saṅghādisesa Kaṇḍa

## 1. Ussayavādikā Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

For the purpose of demonstrating the procedures for rehabilitation from an offense when bhikkhunīs have committed a Saṅghādisesa offense, the identification of the person was made as, "This bhikkhunī... has committed an offense." Intending a meaning different from a Pārājika offense, the name of the offense was taken as "Saṅghādisesa involving rehabilitation (nissāraṇīya)." There is a commentary text (Aṭṭhakathā pāṭha) stating: "The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to the first Kathina training rule; however, this training rule consists merely of the act (kiriya)."

## The Commentary on the Ussayavādikā Training Rule ends.

## 2. Corivuṭṭhāpikā Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

For a bhikkhunī who (ordains a female thief) while remaining seated in the very place where she was sitting without going anywhere else, the offense arises due to speech and mind. For a bhikkhunī who goes to a place such as a specific boundary (khaṇḍasīmā), the offense arises due to body, speech, and mind.

## The Commentary on the Corivuṭṭhāpikā Training Rule ends.

## 3. Ekagāmantaragamana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

Because it is stated as "without intention (ābhoga)," there is no offense if there is intention. In this training rule, it is stated in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary that an offense is committed upon crossing the precinct (upacāra); however, in this Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary, it is stated that an offense is committed upon entering (another village). In both cases, the intended meaning is essentially the same, because the Saṅghādisesa for going to another village is stated with reference to the precinct. Lagging behind from the group of bhikkhunīs is the opposite case. This word "in the forest" is taught according to its literal sense; it also occurs in the case of another village.

By virtue of the verse "Sikkhāpadā buddhavarena vaṇṇitā," the commentary also mentions the opposite bank of a river as being included within another village.

## The Commentary on the Ekagāmantaragamana Training Rule ends.
112:
The statement "An offense of wrong-doing (dukkata) is committed due to concealing"—

Contradicts the verse (Parivāra, 481): "One falls into a grave offense (garuka) that is remediable (sāvasesa); one conceals it out of disrespect; she is neither a bhikkhunī nor would she be touched by the fault; this problem has been reflected upon by the wise."

Therefore, as it appears like a clerical error (pamādalekhā) in this context, the appropriate meaning should be sought.

In the section on penance (Mānatta) for monks, it is stated: "Beyond the distance of two stone-throws from the enclosure of a fenced monastery, or from a place suitable for an enclosure in an unfenced monastery." However, in this section for bhikkhunīs, it is stated: "Two stone-throws from the village precinct (upacāra) and from the monks' monastery precinct," and so forth.

In that regard, for monks, it is allowable to perform that act of penance even in a village after crossing the aforementioned area. For bhikkhunīs, however, it is not allowable in a village. Some say this is why it is stated thus. Other teachers say it is not allowable for monks in a village either. A monks' monastery is established having already crossed the village precinct; therefore, the monastery precinct alone was mentioned below without mentioning the village. A bhikkhunīs' monastery is allowable only within a village and not outside; therefore, both the village precinct and the monastery precinct are shown here. Thus, they say that in both cases, there is no difference in the intended meaning. The appropriate statement should be accepted.

## The Commentary on Saṅghādisesa ends.
113:
## Nissaggiya Kaṇḍa

In the second training rule (Akālacīvarabhājana), the out-of-season robe obtained through distribution is a Nissaggiya (to be forfeited). Even after performing the Vinaya procedure and forfeiting that robe, it cannot be obtained (taken) by the person who distributed it.

In the third training rule (Cīvaraparivattana), there is a text stating: "The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to the taking of what is not given (adinnādāna); however, this involves painful feeling (dukkhavedanā)."

In the fourth training rule (Aññaviññāpana), if one does not receive the object originally requested but receives another object of even lesser value, it is still a Nissaggiya because the factors (anga) are fulfilled.

## The Commentary on Nissaggiya ends.
114:
## Pācittiya Kaṇḍa

## 1. Paṭhamavagga Vaṇṇanā

In the first training rule regarding garlic (Lasuṇa), garlic with green leaves is called Haritaka. Cāpalasuṇa is garlic without segments (cloves). In fact, it has only a sprout. Onions (Palaṇḍuka) and so forth are allowable by their very nature. It is written that it is allowable to use them not only in cooking soup and so forth, but even in gruel or rice at the very least. There is a view of the Abhayagiri sect that: "Garlic is allowable for a sick bhikkhunī only during the morning mealtime; it is not allowable for one who is not sick."

In the second training rule regarding hair in the private area (Sambādhaloma), it is allowable to have the hair removed after asking the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs on account of an illness. In this training rule and in the garlic training rule, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkata) occurs for a male monk.

In the seventh training rule regarding raw grain (Āmakadhañña), there is a commentary text stating: "The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to the training rule on traveling on a high road (Addhānamagga)."

In the ninth (eighth) training rule, 'kuṭṭa' means the wall of a house. 'Pākāra' means an enclosure wall.

'Chaḍḍitakhetta' refers to an old (harvested) field. In a field belonging to the Saṅgha, it is allowable for a monk to discard rubbish and so forth because it is included in the Saṅgha's property. For bhikkhunīs as well, it is allowable in a field belonging to the Saṅgha or the Bhikkhu-Saṅgha in the same manner as already stated. It is written that although it is allowable, it should be done in a proper and suitable manner.

In the tenth training rule regarding dancing and singing (Naccagīta), the statement "performing those acts of dancing etc. oneself" is not directly in this training rule. Why? Because it has the origin of sheep's wool (eḷakalomasamuṭṭhāna). If it is not there, why is it mentioned? It is because of the Great Authority (Mahāpadesa) consistent with the Suttas. If one is not even allowed to go to see or hear dancing and so forth, how much more so is one not allowed to perform it oneself—this is mentioned because it can be obtained through this method of reasoning. Otherwise, the Great Authorities would be useless. "In this way, the method should be applied in other cases as well. Regarding the origin (samuṭṭhāna), one should not take only what is stated here, but should take it by way of the six origins," say the teachers. Other teachers say, "The origin stated here is only for the offense occurring during the act of going to see or hear, which is the root; therefore, it is only the sheep's wool origin."

"Standing in the monastery (ārāma)" does not mean only standing; rather, it includes going there and seeing or hearing in all four postures. "One who is standing in the monastery" means one who is included within the monastery. Otherwise, a bhikkhunī sitting in the monastery would not be prohibited from seeing or hearing.

## The Commentary on the First Group ends.

In the eleventh training rule (Pārivāsika), "without relinquishing consent" means remaining without saying the words for relinquishing consent, such as "Go as you please." The decision in this training rule is as follows: Extracting the phrase "by the giving of consent for one undergoing probation" (pārivāsika-chanda-dāna), the word-analysis (padabhājanī) "by the assembly that has risen" (vuṭṭhitāya parisāya) was taught. Regarding that Pali text, it is explained in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary: "'By the assembly that has risen' means departing from the assembly by relinquishing consent through body, speech, or by the mere act of relinquishing consent." Here, however, it means that because consent is not relinquished, it is proper to perform the formal act. Therefore, it is written that it is proper to remain within the twelve-cubit forearm's length (hatthapāsa) without relinquishing consent and to assemble again to perform the formal act.

## Commentary on the Decision on Origination
Regarding the decision on originations (samuṭṭhāna), because mountain-top festivals (giraggasamajja) and so forth are called "unintentional worldly faults" (acittaka-lokavajja), they are unintentional (acittaka) because an offense is incurred by watching or anointing without knowing it is "dancing" or "perfume," thus being a mind that does not know the object (vatthu). For a bhikkhunī who watches or anoints while knowing it is "dancing" or "perfume," they are worldly faults (lokavajja) precisely because it is unwholesome. Acts such as ordaining a female thief (corivuṭṭhāpana) are intentional (sacittaka) because an offense is incurred only when one performs the act while knowing the object as "a thief" and so forth. Acts such as higher ordination (upasampadā) are prescribed faults (paṇṇattivajja) because they should not be performed with an exclusively unwholesome mind. It is written: "In the case of this training rule, the state of being intentional or unintentional should be taken by the knowledge or ignorance of the object (vatthu), not by the knowledge or ignorance of the regulation (paṇṇatti)." Since the intended meaning is not shown in brief:

The state of being unintentional is known in two ways: ignorance of the object and ignorance of the regulation.
Knowledge is said here to be of two kinds: not knowing by its own name,
And knowing by another name; knowledge of the object is of one kind in cases of force,
And of one kind in equal conduct; in that [other name], that knowledge is connected.
Knowing by another name is known in two ways: one in objects like pearls and so forth,
And one in parts like hair and so forth; thus this distinction should be understood.

The remaining meaning here is clear. Because the decision has already been stated for the unclear meanings, it is not extracted again.

Of these two, sammukhāvinaya is as previously described. Performing the yebhuyyasika act is called yebhuyyasikā-samatha. Thus, a legal issue of dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa) is settled by these two methods of settlement.

A legal issue of accusation (anuvādādhikaraṇa) is settled by four methods of settlement: sammukhāvinaya, sativinaya, amūḷhavinaya, and tassapāpiyasikā. In a legal issue of accusation settled by sammukhāvinaya-samatha alone, the words of the accuser and the accused are heard. If there is no offense, both are made to forgive each other; if there is an offense, it is decided as "In this case, such and such an offense has occurred," and thus it is settled. In such a settlement, the characteristic of sammukhāvinaya is as previously described.

When an Arahant monk is accused of a groundless failure in virtue (sīla-vipatti), and that monk requests a verdict of mindfulness (sativinaya), the Saṅgha grants the sativinaya by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (ñatti-catuttha-kammavācā). At that time, it is settled by both sammukhāvinaya and sativinaya. Once the sativinaya has been granted, a further accusation against that Arahant person is no longer valid.
